subsubtopic: DISABILITY PENSIONS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to seek unanimous consent to move a motion under Standing Order 43. Having regard to the persistent delays in applications for veterans disability pensions being dealt with by the Pension Commission, and as the entitlement and review board work load has reached emergency proportions, and consideration must be given to a means of speeding up the process, particularly for those veterans who are in their late years, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Madill):
That the matter be immediately referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs to review those clauses in the legislation, and particularly the benefit of the doubt clause and as well the shortage of administrative personnel, to relieve the excessive waiting period which is causing hardship to many thousands of veterans.

subsubtopic: POLICY REVIEW STUDIES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising from the recent indiscretions committed by the Globe and Mail and Le Soleil in respect of confidential studies of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes):
That the House recommend to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to consider prompt release of the complete set of recently prepared studies in his department dealing with policy
review of the Atlantic region, the prairie region and the Pacific region before the daily press gets its hands on these reports,'thus ripping off the taxpayers of Canada by publishing the government's confidential documents.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Minister of Supply and Services):
subsubtopic: CANADIAN COMMERCIAL CORPORATION-SALE OF AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The transaction involves the sale of surplus and non-surplus materiel to a foreign government with the proceeds of the sale to be used to purchase further supplies for National Defence. At the direction of the Governor in Council and the Minister of Supply and Services, both facets are being handled by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. The financial aspects of the transaction are being administered in accordance with the provisions of relevant legislation and have been approved by Treasury Board on the advice of their legal advisers, the Department of Justice, as follows: 1. (a) Proceeds received from the sale of surplus material are being retained by the Canadian Commercial Corporation as it is authorized to do by the CCC Act, and are being used to purchase materiel for the Department of National Defence; (b) proceeds received from the sale of non-surplus materiel are being administered in accordance with Section 11 of the National Defence Act.
2.	No, they are being retained and administered by the Canadian Commercial Corporation in accordance with Sections 3 and 5 of the CCC Act in furthering the corporation's purposes; in this instance, the purchase of defence materiel.

Note: The importation of exotic cattle is dealt with by "importation year". Within this year, a shipment enters quarantine on Grosse lie in October and shipments enter quarantine on St. Pierre in November and the following May.
2.	Applicants provide written "project proposals" outlining their proposed breeding program utilizing the cattle for which they are making application to import and provide an inventory of their present cattle herd with particular reference to those cattle of European breeding.
[Mr Richardson.]
A departmental officer visits and interviews each applicant to verify the cattle inventory, and provide an assessment as to his capabilities and the likelihood of his achieving a viable breeding program. These project proposals and interview reports are then submitted anonymously to a technical review committee composed for four geneticists, two of whom are from this Department and two of whom are from universities. The committee assesses and rates the project proposals on the likelihood of the project proposal leading to a viable herd development of general improvement to the livestock industry in Canada, and the likelihood of the breeding proposal being achieved. The permits are then allocated to those importers whose proposals receive the higher ratings until such time as the limits of the quarantine stations are reached. The number of cattle awarded to each applicant is dependent upon the priorities recommended by the technical review committee and the rating awarded the proposal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to conclude the remarks I began on Friday. I regret the absence from the House of the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) who spoke the other day, because I wanted to refer in part to some of the statements he made in this debate.
If I understood the minister correctly, he indicated some sort of opposition to the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) because he seemed to be concerned about the fact that that amendment will make the declaration of these principles too firm. If I may use the exact language which was adopted by the Minister of Communications, he said that the principles would then not be "flexible and subject to change". That is the point. The substantive purpose of these principles is to provide some guarantee of application, a guarantee both to persons who are already in the public service and, just as important, a guarantee to persons who might contemplate joining the public service. That is necessary precisely because there is a widespread apprehension that previously the rules either were not known or were not applied in a satisfactory or fair way.
The minister now asks for flexibility. But it is fair for us to ask: flexibility in what direction? Flexibility for whom? The very reason that we face this substantive issue now is precisely that there was a kind of flexibility which seemed unfair to many people. The amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition would guard against that kind of flexibility. It would provide some guarantees. The resolution without it would be mere opinion.
It might be claimed that it is influential opinion. But may I remind you and the House that influential opinion also changes. For a public servant, or for a young constituent of mine who might contemplate becoming a public servant, there would be cold comfort if an election or some other event caused this opinion to change or to be ignored, because there is no doubt at all that in law the opinion expressed in a resolution has no force. That is the clear result of the case of Roman Corporation versus Hudson's Bay which was decided in the Ontario Court of Appeal and upheld in the Supreme Court of Canada this May. It made the point firmly that proceedings in this parliament have no force in law. It is clear from the advice of the Chairman of the Public Service Commission that, in his actions, he was bound only by the language of the act of parliament and not by the language of the so-called Pearson pledge which had no force in law.
It is clear even in the recent statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) who explicitly advised the House that his government did not intend to be bound by a mere resolution of the House concerning Viet Nam. The precedents of law, indeed the very practices of ministers of the government this session, affirm
June 4, 1973

the fact that in terms of law the opinion of this parliament is as incidental as a cough in the night. There is no doubt about that. There is no guarantee in this resolution without the amendment, no protection over a period of time, and it has no more force than the statement of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) in December or the pledge of the late prime minister years before.
The minister asks for flexibility. If that is a serious request, it raises important questions indeed about what other matters the government might excuse from legislation with the argument that flexibility is needed. What matter before this parliament is so fixed and firm that it does not require flexibility? That, Sir, is what the process of amendment is all about. The extra advantage of the amendment is the requirement that any changes, any flexibility, must be accomplished in the light of day, with the knowledge and deliberate consent of the parliament and people involved. And until that consent is achieved, the people concerned have guarantees. I ask you, Sir, what is so special about this matter that the normal practices cannot apply?
The minister suggested that this matter is very difficult to be definite about, involving as it does staff relations and subjective judgments. He went on to suggest-he didn't come right out and say it, but the implication was clear-that the application of language guidelines is so complex that only the people who actually apply them know enough to criticize. There is an argument with possibilities. If we accept that view, then this parliament would be mute. There would be no criticism or scrutiny of anything, and no control.
The government will have to find a better defence than to suggest that matters are so complex that only it can deal with them. Of course they are complex, but either you are going to have guidelines or you are not, and if we have a situation where an administration or an administrator is able to modify a guideline because it is too difficult to enforce, then again we have no guarantees at all.
The minister pointed out that spokesmen for this party had argued, when the Languages Act was first before parliament, for an approach by resolution because that would allow flexibility. That, Sir, is a mere debating point, and matters relating to official bilingualism are too important to be dealt with by debating points. In any event, the government rejected then the approach it proposes now, and the practice was established of proceeding by law, not by resolution, on this question. If the substance of the matter is important enough to be enshrined in law, so are the principles which guide the application of bilingualism in the public service. The government just cannot have it both ways.
But if the minister is serious, and if we grant his request for flexibility, we will again create conditions in which public servants or prospective public servants will fear that regulations will be interpreted against their interests. That is the very fear this resolution purports to redress, yet if we reject this amendment we run the risk of reviving the fear instead of reducing it. In light of all that I have said I assume the minister was not serious in his suggestion on Friday. He was not stating the government's response so much as he was testing the wind. Certainly, if he is interested in allaying fears, achieving bilingualism
Official Languages
and getting on with the business of Canada, he and his colleagues will support the amendment and give force to what they propose.
As the House knows, this matter of bilingualism is not without contention. In my own region of western Canada there are some who, as a matter of what they see as principle, would oppose virtually any measure designed to make bilingualism work. In my view they are the voices of a small minority, and are no more representative of that region than the voices of separatism are representative of Quebec.

Indeed, Sir, they are probably less so. But I say with seriousness that there are other western Canadians, many in number, who have reservations about the application of official bilingualism but who will go along with it as part of the price they pay for the other benefits of their country. With time and with encouragement, many of the sons and daughters of this group will become bilingual, and some of the group themselves will, because that will be part of being Canadian, like learning to pronounce Mahavolich, or learning to live with snow. But if instead of being encouraged to accept bilingualism these people are encouraged to suspect it, there is the danger that they will become stubborn; that is the danger directly aroused by this debate. The problem is not the nine principles. It is not even the DeBane addendum or amendment. The problem is the public tone and the suggested motives for the introduction of the resolution.
When I began my remarks on Friday, I referred to my own regret at the innuendo in the remarks in January of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). That, Sir, was an insult to me and to many other members who deliberately faced down the temptation to embrace prejudice on this question. But more than an insult, these insinuations set poison in the system. A predictable response has come from that small minority which actively opposes bilingualism. But the poison could spread to other and more tolerant parts of the body politic, particularly if the innuendos continue and if the government rejects an amendment which merely gives the binding force of law to what it proposes.
I do not give this warning lightly. As I listened to the Minister of Cummunications (Mr. Pelletier) on Friday with his talk of dinosaurs and his playing with the monarchy, I wondered what effort he has made to understand my part of the country. I have tried to understand his, and so have several of my colleagues here as well as my neighbours at home.

It was not easy for us who came from cities and towns where there were no French Canadians, from areas far from Quebec, and who attended schools where French is not properly taught. That problem still exists.

But we are doing the positive things we can. Sir, we have a right to expect not patience but reciprocity, at least from a minister of the Crown, some fairness, and some

sensitivity to matters which might cause us special problems. National unity is not a one-way street.

Sir, we in western Canada are not a region like the others. No region in this country, is, but one of our characteristics is a cultural and linguistic tradition different from that of the longer settled regions of the country. A great many of our citizens are of an origin other than English or French, and to many of them bilingualism appeared as a threat, particularly when the government delayed so long its recognition of multiculturalism. Many more of us, my age and older, were raised in a kind of regional insularity in which we just did not know that Canada, in practice, was a bilingual country. Indeed, I was out of high school before that fact came home to me. So bilingualism was, quite literally, a world we did not know, and the adjustment to the Languages Act was not as natural in Alberta as it might have been in Montreal.
There are still some special fears. One is that western Canada's young men and women of talent might not enjoy an equal chance in Canada's public service simply because they were born where the French language was inadequately taught. Whether it is paranoia or perceptiveness, many western Canadians feel at a disadvantage anyway, in competition for position against the old school, old boy network of central Canada, and that sense is sharpened by the knowledge that some public service positions require a level of bilingualism it is often difficult for prairie candidates to acquire. The amendment of the Leader of the Opposition would provide some guarantees against that fear, but it is symptomatic of a western sensitivity which the program of bilingualism must recognize if it is to succeed. Sir, that sensitivity is not quieted, but aroused, by insinuations of the kind in which too many ministers have indulged.
When I began to speak on Friday, I expressed my surprise at the insistence of the government on bringing this matter back and expressed by regretful conclusion that their motive in so doing must have been to seek some means to divide my party, even if, in the attempt, they divided the country, too. That might not be their motive. Perhaps, in fact, they seek only to extend guarantees to the public service. If that is so, they will support the amendment because only the amendment contains guarantees. If their interest instead is division, they will oppose the amendment. But even if they do that, there is no way they will reduce or muddy the clear commitment of this party to a united and bilingual Canada.

That commitment is not only clear upon the record. It has been proven in the heat of campaigns and in the face of provocation.
In closing today I want to repeat that I, and most of my colleagues, came here with the expectation that the issue of language was essentially settled in Canada, and that we could turn to the urgent concerns of this year and of years to come. We came here to deal with the issues of the

seventies and beyond, and not to strike old poses or fight old wars. That is clearly the desire of the millions of Canadians who grew into adulthood in the fifties and the sixties. It is clearly my mandate from my constituents. We are a new parliament in a new decade with enough contemporary challenges that we need not look back. The best proof the government can offer that it shares this spirit too, that it is more interested in the future than the past, is to support this amendment, which accords with and confirms all the high ideals the Prime Minister spoke of, and then let parliament get on with the other urgent work of 1973.

speechtext:
That was dealt with in a debate four or five years ago. The purpose is to express a view upon the application of that act, in practice, to the public service of this country. I want to take issue with the interjection of the right hon. gentleman. The purpose is to review the basis on which the Official Languages Act is to apply to the public service of this country. The object is to give the House of Commons an occasion to pronounce itself upon institutional bilingualism as it is meant to work in practice. The principles set forth by my colleague the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) outline the blueprint which the government and the Chairman of the Public Service Commission of Canada intend to apply in co-operation with the staff associations. It has also as its purpose the endorsement of those principles by this House and, by reason of this resolution, to take them beyond the dictates of ministerial discretion. I will deal with the argument of the hon. member who preceded me in a few moments but if I may, I should like to deal first with a few general points.
First of all, what do we mean when we talk about bilingualism in the public service? Many of us have said this before but I believe it will bear repeating because the thrust of the policy has been misunderstood in many parts of the country. We are not talking about individual bilingualism, Mr. Speaker; we are not talking about the ability of any Canadian to speak both languages; we are not
June 4, 1973

talking about any type of compulsion to force Canadians to speak the other official language, to speak other than the language that is his mother tongue or his choice. We are talking about what we have called earlier institutional bilingualism. My colleague, the President of the Treasury Board, called it functional bilingualism or the availability of a federal government service to Canadians in either of the two official languages of this country, French or English. In a reciprocal fashion it is the right of every Canadian to work in the public service in either French or English. In other words, it is an institutional fabric by which we hope that the national unity of this country can be cemented-namely the right of any Canadian from any part of Canada to deal with his or her federal government or agencies of the federal government in the language of his or her choice and to allow any Canadian to be involved and to work in the public service in either French or English. As my colleague put it, in a very detailed speech to this House on Friday, it thereby preserves the right of any Canadian to remain unilingual if he wants in his dealings with the Public Service of Canada and unilingual in his service to his country.
What is the purpose of the bilingualism policy? I think every member of the House is highly cognizant of it. Certainly, I was impressed by the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and their appraisal of the situation. National unity is consecrated by the ability of all Canadians to deal with the federal government or work for the federal government in either French or English. National unity in the sense of cultivating a feeling of consecrating the reality, particularly, and let us admit it, among French speaking Canadians, that they have an equal opportunity in this country and that they can be made to feel at home in this country and to feel at home at work or at play in the national capital. It is only in this way that I believe this parliament can undercut one of the arguments of the separatists, namely that only within his own nation state can the French speaking Canadian find his true home, fulfil his true personality, find his complete acceptance.
I believe that if this resolution, which has the support of the House, is applied by the Public Service Commission and by the Treasury Board in co-operation with the staff associations with understanding and humanity and recognition of the human careers that are involved, then the temptation of French speaking Canadians to opt for their own state will not be nearly as attractive. If French speaking Canadians are made to feel at home in reality, in appearance and in psychology within the bosom of a country we call Canada.

Looking through the principles, one can see clarification and protection in a number of distinct areas. There is a new procedure of prior identification and designation of bilingual positions. This gives members of the public service advance notice on which to exercise various career options. There is guaranteed protection for acquired rights of unilingual public servants having ten years of service at the date of Mr. Pearson's original statement in the House. There is a new flexibility in the definition of bilingualism, as it may be required for particular positions. The ability to qualify for a position that may be designated as bilingual is now enshrined in advance of acquiring the second language. In other words, the public servant does not necessarily have to have a capacity in both languages at the time he stands and qualifies for a bilingual position. Once having achieved that position, he is given the opportunity to establish that bilingual qualification. As a result, and this is another point, there is now a wider availability of language training, and it becomes incumbent now on the government to ensure that anyone seeking admission to the public service or seeking promotion within the public service has available to him as of right, no matter what his standing in the hierarchy of the system may be, the necessary language training. Finally, there are wider avenues of appeal respecting the implementation of this policy.

Let me say this to the House about the implementation of the principles. The implementation of the principles can take effect without legislative action. Section 39 of the Public Service Employment Act provides:
In any case where the Commission decides that it is not practicable nor in the best interests of the public service to apply this Act or any provision thereof to any position or person or class of positions or persons, the Commission may, with the approval of the Governor in Council exclude such position or person or class of positions or persons in whole or in part from the operation of this Act; and the Commission may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, re-apply any of the provisions of this Act to any position or person so excluded.
Thus, I submit parliament has already anticipated a possible need for excluding from certain portions of the Public Service Employment Act certain positions or persons. Legislation is, therefore, unnecessary, as the existing laws provide for the implementation of the principle, either by means of the Public Service Employment Act, the Financial Administration Act or the Official Languages Act.
In the past, Mr. Speaker, the Public Service Commission has been reluctant to seek such exclusions under Section 39, but with the approval of this resolution the Chairman of the Public Service Commission and the Commission will interpret this approval as parliament's direction that Section 39 of the Public Service Employment Act be invoked. The Chairman of the Public Service Commission has already advised the staff side of the National Joint Council to this effect and the Public Service Commission will be requesting the Governor in Council to pass regulations under Section 39 to give effect to the principles.
A permanent committee of the National Joint Council, representing the people of Canada and parliament as employer and the staff associations as employees, has been established to keep under constant review matters related to the principles and measures contained in the resolution. It is safe to say that the staff side, recognizing the dynamic nature of this issue, has not pressed for inclusion of the principles in legislation. They believe and we believe that legislation at this time would be inappropriate as the consultation process is working effectively and is responsive to the dynamic nature of the complex issues involved.
The purpose of putting the resolution before the House was not only to re-affirm the government's intention and commitment to the contents of the principles and measures contained in the resolution, but also to seek similar affirmation and commitment from all parties of the House so that the House would support what has already been jointly agreed to between the employer and the staff
June 4, 1973

associations. Through the vehicle of the National Joint Commission, it will remain under continual scrutiny.
I have had a personal commitment for some time to the principles of bilingualism in this country. I had the responsibility for negotiating the Official Languages Act with the attorneys general of the provinces, particularly the provinces in western Canada and Quebec. I had some responsibility for negotiating its passage through parliament. I spoke during the Speech from the Throne debate on January 9, and have tried to give voice to my feelings on this crucial subject on every occasion when I found it legitimate to do so.
I believe that the resolution enshrines a series of principles in the application of the Official Languages Act that are fundamental to national unity. I believe the English speaking majority in this country must try to understand the hopes and feelings of the minority in terms of the future of this country. The French speaking minority must try, on their part, to understand the intense tolerance of the English speaking majority and the considerable progress that has been made in order to equalize opportunities within the Public Service of Canada.
I do not for a moment underestimate the human difficulties encountered in trying to make this policy work. It must work and it must work fairly. It must work because the future of this country is at stake. It must work fairly because we are dealing with men and women who are dedicating their lives to the public service of their country. In terms of the constituency and region I represent, nowhere is it more important that these principles be made to work. As I have said to my constituents on several occasions, without national unity, without a country, the city of Ottawa does not make any sense at all. We in the capital have a special burden, and yet a unique challenge to make it happen and make it work.
Re-affirmation in this House of Commons of these specific principles to convert the theory of the Official Languages Act into practice and working rules will, in my submission, go far toward re-assuring both those who fear bilingualism in the public service is going ahead too fast and those who are concerned that it is not going ahead fast enough. No one has ever claimed that the implementation of this policy would be easy nor that it would not arouse apprehension. The purpose of this resolution is to attempt to relieve that apprehension. Nor has it been claimed that it would not add to the cost of government. It is one of the prices we pay for being Canadian. I believe it is a price well worth paying against the limitless prospects of a united country.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The House has always been considerate, except on one occasion when the present Postmaster General (Mr. Ouellet) was the only person in the House to say "no". If he were here, I would read him some interesting things.
That was one of our arguments. The other was that the Commissioner of Languages has powers that were too great. Lo and behold, some of the Liberal members have since concluded that his powers were too great. He was given greater powers than any person in Canadian history. I heard him yesterday on "Cross Country Checkup". If you really want to check up on what he said yesterday you will have an opportunity of doing that on a later occasion, as I am now speaking on the amendment. He is the one who spoke about the Westmount Rhodesians. That was a classic phrase. He went to the United States to make that statement before a learned society. When he was questioned, he said "I was joking". Joking! Yesterday he was not joking when he was asked questions. He said to one person "garbage" when that person took some issue with the act. He used some other language too that indicated he is completely comtemptuous of the rights that he has and he has come to the position where he believes that anything he does is humorous, regardless of the wrong that has been done to the public service of our country.
We said that the despotic powers of the commissioner should be reduced. We said that there should be protection of the rights of English speaking civil servants who have been in the civil service for years, who could not meet the provisions of the Languages Act and therefore would be denied advancement. I said that bill created an injustice to the people of other racial origins and made them second class citizens. And it did. They were in a lower category, Now, along comes the government and suddenly the Prime Minister has seen the light again, and about $10 million is going to be made available. Some 5 per cent of what is going to be spent on biculturalism and bilingualism is going to be doled out from the rich man's table to all the six million people of racial origins other than English and French.
Sir, I can never get over the observation that the Prime Minister made when somebody asked, "What is going to happen if any civil servant refuses to learn French?" And he replied, "Unwilling? That would be fine. We would keep him running elevators where there are no French Canadians." There is the attitude, Mr. Speaker. And Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition is to say by its vote that we do appreciate the way in which this act has been administered, the way in which discrimination has been practised under it. Sir, I shall not participate in giving to the government the appreciation of one who has tried through the years to bring about an end to discrimination within this nation, and in saying to the Prime Minister and to the

June 4, 1973
Official Languages
government, "We know that you have become transfigured, and that all now is well. You are forgiven."
I opposed the bill. I oppose this resolution on the ground that it will give explicit approval and an expression of confidence to the Prime Minister for doing that which he has not done. Never before has a government ever asked to receive a vote of confidence for what it hasn't done because it has decided since an election to change its mind. I ask hon. members behind me, are you going to be made dupes? I can look at one of you, act one and another who were elected just because of the Languages Act, at least according to the Minister of Transport, and according to two or three other ministers.
This resolution shows a contempt for parliament, for parliament is only consulted when given an opportunity to afford a mechanism for political expediency to the Prime Minister. And he hopes for support of the public. It is not a very subtle plan. The ruse is far too transparent. I, for one, have not that confidence in this government that I will give it support for what it has not done. I shall not support such political trickery.
The purpose is to accomplish the unique feat of conveying to French Canada the idea that absolute bilingualism will prevail. That will be the interpretation. When the Conservative party supports this, French Canada may simply say, "Why should we support that party? Just because it agreed with the action taken by the government?"
On the one hand, government ministers are trying to fool French Canadians, and on the other hand they are pretending to the rest of Canada that they have changed their attitude. I have tried, Sir, with the appreciation that I have for this House, to remove the verbal veneer with which the Prime Minister has endeavoured to clothe this act of expediency. When this Opposition votes for the resolution, every last one of you, according to the Minister of Transport, according to the Minister of Communications, and according to the Postmaster General, will have voted for the Act. None of you will be able to go to your constituencies and meet that. That will be the Liberal argument in every part of this country.
The Conservative party tried to improve the Official Languages Act. They were spurned. I am not going to ask hon. members to read the Official Languages Act but I venture an opinion, even without benefit of a Gallup Poll, that it has not been read by very many. It has never been my custom-and at my age I live from day to day-to tailor my principles to political expediency. I do not intent to cower before false gods. This is a transparent trick.
Sir, I spent a lifetime trying to bring about equality for all Canadians of all racial origins. Now, this will be swept aside. Because I was of mixed origin I felt for others who were too. My people had been in Canada since the early 1800's, but because of my name I was not a Canadian. I was not accepted as a Canadian. I put an end to that. I said we were Canadians all.
And what have we got today? We have Anglophones, Francophones, multiculturalphones, all kinds. Everything I have striven for I see now being swept aside, and an end to that Canadianism which, above everything else, has been my devotion throughout a long life. It could be the

last time I will speak on this subject when this debate is over, but my last words will be: God help Canada from the disunity in which it now finds itself.
We shall never build the nation which our potential resources make possible by dividing ourselves into Anglophones, Francophones, multiculturalphones, or whatever kind of phoneys you choose. I say: Canadians, first, last, and always!

Mr. Speaker, I have been a great admirer of the right hon. gentleman. I think this is an open secret in the House of Commons. I still am. I think that the right hon. gentleman has earned his place in the history books of this country by his contribution to parliament, by his production of the Bill of Rights, by his undeniable concern for the rights of individuals. Parliament would be a poorer place without the right hon. gentleman. His ability as a debater is second to none and his ability to talk around the subject at hand is second to none. Very rarely this afternoon did the right hon. gentleman speak about the issue at hand. His concept of equality is something that is hard for me to follow. Equality for Canadians, obviously in the opinion of the right hon. gentleman, means a unilingual English-speaking Canadian, a Canada in which Ottawa and the public service is out of bounds to millions of Canadians who happen to live in one particular section of the country called the province of Quebec.
The hon. gentleman has done many things to advance the cause of French speaking Canadians. He did, indeed, name the first French speaking Governor General in Canadian history, following the first English speaking Canadian Governor General in Canadian history which I think was obviously a very logical thing to do. But when we get down to an issue as sensitive as language, when we get down to the question of unity, I try very hard to follow the logic of the right hon. gentleman. For many years I have attempted to be in the House on each and every occasion when he debates because I have learned a great deal from his style and his ability to make speeches without reading a text, something which should be enforced in this House. Nevertheless, I was puzzled and found it difficult to understand how his concept of Canadianism could possibly be acceptable to the people who are resident of the province of Quebec, who are Canadian, whose mother tongue happens to be French and who are told "There is room for you in Ottawa but under the following condition-that you learn to speak English because that is the language of the majority in this country."

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman, subtlely and astutely, dragged in the two nations concept, the associate state concept, the third force, people of other cultures and things that had nothing at all to do with the issue at hand,

which is the application of the Official Languages Act in an appropriate manner. There are many people who feel that this act has not been applied with enough vigour and who feel that the progress has been slow. I do not share that opinion. I came here in 1962 when members of the Creditiste Party speaking against were the statement of the President of the Canadian National Railways to the effect that the French speaking Canadians were not capable of being directors of a Canadian corporation called the CNR.
I lived in Quebec when we went through the evaluation of the 60's and the two nations concept as the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) knows. I used to stand in this House in 1962, 1963 and 1964 and fight against those very principles and I used to be told "You are stupid-as a politician you won't get re-elected in your constituency which is 80 per cent French by denying the two nations concept". I used to say "Be damned on re-election" and fight it and I accused the provincial government of the day of fostering separatism under different titles and under different slogans. So, I bow not even to the right hon. gentleman when it comes to my concern for this country, to my appreciation of the French speaking Canadians of Canada. If I were a French speaking Canadian, I would have been a separatist when I was young and I would have been a separatist in 1962 when I came here. At that time I was appalled to find that the only gesture of friendship in the House of Commons was that of simultaneous translation. Beyond that I can remember the days when Hansard was not even printed in the French language, when the reports of committee hearings in French were tabled weeks later and when we spent day after day apologizing for the lack of linguistic capabilities in the House of Commons.
Last Wednesday and Thursday, with the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe and the hon. member for Drummond (Mr. Boisvert), I met a group of young French speaking Canadians from my riding out on the lawn and they asked all sorts of questions about Ottawa and about parliament. One said to the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, "How is it that when I come to Ottawa to visit parliament I am greeted in French?" I can remember the day when it was not so, when we could not find enough bilingual people at the front door to take the tours from Quebec around the House of Commons. That was not too many years ago.
Mr. Speaker, what are we asking French speaking Canadians to do? What is the Prime Minister suggesting? Nothing more than that Canadians whose mother tongue happens to be French should be able to participate in the public service of the country, to realize that there is room for them in the public service of this country, to realize that there is opportunity for them to be promoted, to make them realize that their language is welcome and enriching rather than a hindrance when they come to this place. We are asking them, I hope, one of these days to stop comparing the affluence of Ottawa with the drudgery and slum conditions of Hull across the river which is what they were expected to do when they came here 20 years ago. They were expected to live across the river, work all day in the English language in Ottawa and then go back home across the river where they could at least be exposed to their own culture. This is not good enough, Mr. Speaker,

for the French Canadian federalists of the province of Quebec who want to participate in everyday life.

Well, I do not want to get into a rereading of the 1968 speeches. I can still remember some of the speeches on the flag debate that were sickening. The hon. gentleman dragged in the flag, dragged in the Union Jack.
I am afraid the hon. gentleman has got an Achilles heel in that he has never been able to understand the French people of the province of Quebec. We came forward with a flag that bore no symbol of the French speaking Canadians, no symbol of the English speaking Canadians, but a simple maple leaf that was as acceptable to those who traced their ancestry to Ireland, to Poland, to the Ukraine, to Italy or any other country. His children or grandchildren have made this such a wonderful country in which to live.
But, Mr. Speaker, if we, and I mean not only the Liberal Party but all federalists in the House of Commons and in Quebec, are to beat back the separatist movement and continue beating it back, and if we are to win our fight for the minds and hearts of the youngsters in the province of Quebec, we must prevent them from turning inward and show them that there are opportunities in Ottawa if they should wish to participate in the development and formation of this country by serving in the public service. Such service is impossible if the penalty they must pay is being denied promotion because their mother tongue is French rather than English.

June 4, 1973
Official Languages
I travelled across this country in 1964 and 1965, and visited Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta. I can say, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) said, that I rarely ran into anybody bigoted or biased in those places. I visited every constituency, I think, in Saskatchewan, including Prince Albert, and in pretty well every riding, people would come up to me and say, "I originated in Quebec" or tell me that the parents or grandparents had come from that province and that they had been able to hang on to their language and culture to varying degrees. Are these people not entitled to be served, at least by their own government, in their own language, regardless of where they live in Canada, if they need to be so served? How else will you persuade French speaking Canadians to leave Quebec and move to Ontario, Alberta, Manitoba, or British Columbia?
It is not too many years ago that one of my closest friends, a French speaking Canadian, turned down a tremendous promotion outside Quebec only three months after leaving the province, because he could not find schooling for his children or cultural outlets, and could not even deal with the federal government in his own language. That is not what we want or what the Canadian people want. Those who happen to be bigoted or biased in their approach, and I am talking about Members of Parliament, and display bias or bigotry in order to be elected, are wrong. What is right eventually becomes politically right. A new generation is growing up, and this type of bigoted approach is fast disappearing.

speechtext: Not in Quebec, with Ouellet calling us royalist fanatics.

speechtext:
At the same time, we must apply the Official Languages Act in a gentlemanlike manner, in a sensitive manner, and not in brusque way, because people, quite logically, fear change. English speaking Quebecers fear change. They are afraid of the working language in their own province being French and of the possibility that new Canadians will be forced to speak another language rather than the one of their own choice. So, the province of Quebec has a stake in this, too, and must make certain that its policies are fair and not discriminatory.
As so many others have said before me, this is the greatest country in the world. We all agree. Even though we are suffering from troubles and are suffering from so-called disunity, there is less trouble of that kind now than there was even ten years ago. Former prime minister Lester Pearson spoke very little French but had the vision to unite this country, to set up the B & B Commission, to take steps needed for the new Canadian flag, and to do the things that were needed with respect to the public service. Our present Prime Minister is carrying on that tradition. The Leader of the Opposition and other members have supported him, because that is only right and fair and is the price we must pay for the continuation of this country. It is a very small price, I might add.
Any country with two official languages and enjoying a multicultural society is rich. Such a country is a contrast to other countries which have eliminated all but one language and assimilated all cultures into one. It is paradoxical, perhaps, that Canadians of Italian, Ukrainian, Russian or Polish descent are better able to cling to their own languages and cultures by reason of the fact that we have

been able to resist being assimilated culturally by the United States. That resistance has been possible because of the existence of several million people in Quebec who do not necessarily share a common language with our neighbour. So, we are all richer because in this country we speak two languages and follow many, many cultures.
In 1973, as we look around the world and see the miseries of other countries, it is gratifying to know that the only thing dividing us is the medium of communication. Why, young people in Europe learn three, four or five languages under their educational curriculum. I hope from now on that this debate will centre on the Official Languages Act, that we do not accuse each other of fostering disharmony and that the Prime Minister will not be accused of being a divisive force, as he was just accused. There is no political gain in this type of approach, nor can anybody gain much by being bigoted or biased in approaching the whole question of language. If any gain results from such an approach, it will be very, very temporary. .
Let me say in conclusion that I could have lived with the amendment of the hon. gentleman of the opposition, although, perhaps, it would have introduced some degree of inflexibility. Perhaps the suggestion contained in the motion should remain vested in regulations which can be adjusted periodically.
Let me say a word about the constitutionality of this whole approach, and whether there are or ought to be two official languages in Canada. Mr. Justice Thorson has made his views on this subject known. I have discussed this subject with the learned judge and read his reasons for his stand, his books and his articles. Frankly, whether this act is constitutional is relatively unimportant. The facts of the case do not stand on the constitution; they stand on reality, on the fact that in Quebec there are millions of Canadians whose mother tongue happens to be French, who want to remain federalist and who want to see this country remain together. In several provincial elections they have rejected the separatist parties. If they are given a significant opportunity, they will become one of the real forces for unity in this country because they are realistic. If we deny them the right to work in their own language, to be promoted in the federal public service or to see the national capital, as it should exist on both sides of the river, as a reflection of our dual nationality and multicultural society, we will play a self-defeating and self-annihilating role. I support the Official Languages Act and commend it to all members of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to express myself fluently in French, but I regret that my French is not good enough for me to do so. I rely on the goodwill and the wisdom of my French-speaking colleagues in asking them to understand why I must continue my comments in English.
I listened with interest to the comments of the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey). I would like to say that I agree with the points he made and express my disappointment with the remarks of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) who accused the government of political trickery in this resolution.
4404

Official Languages
The right hon. member for Prince Albert said the resolution was designed to fool French Canadians into thinking the resolution was significant and a trick to convince English speaking Canadians that the government had really changed its attitude. I am disappointed that the debate is being continued on that level because there is a problem in Canada in the public service and with the Official Languages Act. I hope this resolution, to some small degree, will be a positive step forward towards correcting the shortcomings of the policy. If the Liberal government had followed the suggestions of my party when the Official Languages Act was first introduced and had consulted with the public service, perhaps we would not have a need for this resolution at this time. I hope this resolution will alleviate some of the problems.
I represent a constituency which is 6 per cent French speaking in the sense the people can trace their origin to French ancestry. This is compared with 40 per cent in the whole of Canada. In this debate, we must not lose sight of the realities of Canadian history and the reality of the situation as it now exists in this country. To those who want a unilingual Canada or to keep Quebec French only, I say they are sadly mistaken about the realities of our times.
If we look at Canadian history, we see there were two founding races. Throughout our history, since the time of the conquest in 1760, the English rulers tried on numerous occasions to assimilate the French Canadians, to make them into English speaking British subjects. They have failed. They failed in 1763 with the proclamation of that date. They failed with the Act of Union in 1840. One thing is clear from the reading of Canadian history. There is within the French Canadians a distinct desire to preserve their culture and identity. We call it "le fait frangais". I think this is a lesson all of us must heed.
I speak of the reality of today. Today, there are six million French speaking Canadians, the majority of whom do not speak any English. I refuse to get into the argument of majority-minority. The fact is that French Canadians are the majority in the province of Quebec and, therefore, have rights. Because they belong to this confederation, to this country, they have rights outside that province, just as English Canadians should have rights within that province.
When we debate this resolution, we must make a distinction between bilingualism and biculturalism and the Official Languages Act. The Official Languages Act, to which this resolution has reference, is but one facet of implementing bilingualism in this country. The Official Languages Act is concerned with linguistic equality in the public service. Bilingualism is a term of much broader scope. The objective of bilingualism is to allow Canadians of either language background to feel at home in the country so that they may truly say "I am a Canadian", not just in the province of Quebec or in English speaking Canada. In order to make them feel at home throughout Canada, we have to do more than is outlined in the Official Languages Act. If this is to be truly a country where people of either language group can feel at home, we have to look to not only government offices throughout

Canada being able to serve people in both languages, but government run transportation facilities as well.
We talk about bilingualism in the hope of achieving much in this country, yet when we look at the situation in our schools, we see there is a backward trend, a decline in the teaching of the French language in English-Canadian schools. In 1971, 55 per cent of the students in English Canada studied French. Today, in 1973, it has declined to 47 per cent and seems to be going down. When I look at those figures, I worry about what the future has in store for Canada and the opportunities for our young people to become familiar with both languages.
I am also concerned about present day attitudes toward the issue of bilingualism, particularly the Official languages Act and the way the government has tried to implement it. In January, I sent a questionnaire to my constituents. I included a question on bilingualism. The question read "In your opinion, is the federal government's policy on bilingualism (a) essential to foster Canadian unity, (b) doing more harm than good." Of those who answered whether they thought bilingualism as being carried out by the government is essential to foster Canadian unity, 30 per cent said yes and 32 per cent said no, almost tied. On the question of whether they thought the present government's policy of bilingualism was doing more harm than good, 55 per cent said yes and 10 per cent said no. The figures do not add up to 100 per cent because many who replied only answered one part of the question.
There definitely seems to be a concern among English speaking Canadians about just what this policy is doing. Based on the replies I received and comments I have heard, there seems to be a great deal of misunderstanding about bilingualism and the Official Languages Act. The responsibility for this misunderstanding must be placed at the door of the government for its failure to convince and explain to English Canadians the necessity of this approach.
Today, we have a backlash among English speaking Canadians and a skepticism among French speaking Canadians as to the worth of the whole measure. I wonder why the implementation of the Official Languages Act is responsible for this unfavourable attitude among many English speaking Canadians. The Official Languages Act is concerned with institutional bilingualism. Its application is limited to those places where it is needed. Each federal department must have enough employees and written materials to provide service to the public in both official languages.
We hear many reasons from English speaking Canadians as to why they object to this act. I think many of them are unfounded. Many people argue that this policy is costly to the taxpayer. The figure of $54 million is bandied about. I do not know whether that figure is accurate. Stories are told by English speaking public servants about not being promoted because they are not bilingual. This goes from neighbour to neighbour and stereotyping begins. What may have been one incident is generalized beyond all proportions. What are the facts? We hear about the cost to the taxpayers. Well, Mr. Speaker, I pose the question: What price Canadian unity? We have many examples of misspending by this government and we have had such examples for years. I don't propose to try to
June 4, 1973

categorize them all, but I merely mention the case of the Bonaventure. To be niggardly and to argue that it costs government money to provide services in both official languages is not only myopic, it is deceiving and it is not worthy for people to argue in this context.
What about the idea that civil servants are being discriminated against because they speak only one language? We in English Canada often get the impression that it is English speaking Canadians who are being discriminated against. Well, I read through the official report of the Commissioner of Official Languages and there are some very interesting statistics in that report of which I hope the public will be made aware. When one looks at the language used by the complainants under the Official Languages Act for the year 1972, one finds that 15 per cent of the complainants are English speaking and 85 per cent are French speaking Canadians. If one looks at the number of admissible complaints under the Act, the vast majority of them are from French speaking Canadians and their complaints have been found to be justified.
In 1971, there were 59,000 civil service jobs filled. Of those 59,000 jobs, 80 per cent required English only. Those requiring French only numbered 8 per cent, and 9 per cent required the use of both languages. In other words, it is ten times harder for French Canadians to get jobs in the civil service. So I say to English speaking Canadians who, through maybe personal experience, although I suspect mostly through hearsay evidence, say that the Official Languages Act is discriminatory, that they should read the statistics and they will then know that it is French Canadians who really have the problem trying to find equality in the civil service. I ask them to try to understand the frustration undergone by the French speaking Canadians who face these circumstances.
At the same time, I must once again-and how often this seems to be the request of English speaking Canadians of French speaking Canadians-ask French speaking Canadians to try to understand and be patient with English speaking civil servants. God knows there have been hundreds of years of injustice done to French speaking Canadians and it cannot be righted overnight. But I sincerely believe that English-speaking Canadians are now beginning to realize that something must be done. If we can only get the facts across to them, then I think they will understand, because the English-speaking civil servants I have talked to are not the bigoted stereotyped civil servants we hear on the media or whom we hear in conversations. I have talked to civil servants in Sault Ste. Marie who do not object to the principle of the Official Languages Act. What they object to is the way it was implemented. I was really impressed by the positive tone they had, the positive outlook they displayed. They saw the need for bilingualism in the civil service and they were willing to take the extra steps to accommodate the policy. But they objected to some bureaucrat saying: This is the way its got to be done. Or someone not explaining fully to them. As a result they were disturbed. They were not angry; they were not bigoted; they were just disturbed and they wanted to see the situation corrected. I find there is a lot of good faith and it is up to the government to do
Official Languages
something about explaining and implementing the policy of bilingualism in the civil service.
Therefore, I welcome these nine points of the resolution as my party welcomes them. I think they will go part way at least towards correcting some of the wrongs which have existed in the implementation of the Official Languages Act. I support the principles. But I do not support the Conservative amendment nor does my party. The Conservative party in its amendment to the resolution argues that the nine principles outlined should be made into several different statutes. As I say we do support the principles. But to try to believe they can be put into statutes will only complicate the problem and result in a backward step. The problem is that in trying to implement a policy one has to take into account particular local circumstances and situations as they develop. But this must be an on-going process. You cannot legislate fixed rules and say that they apply in Sault Ste. Marie and in every other community in exactly the same way. So these principles, if they are not made into statutes, will enable us to have some flexibility.
That there is need for flexibility was recognized by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) himself when he said, and I quote: "These guidelines have to be and should be flexible and they have to be subject to change". We believe in that principle, Mr. Speaker, and not only our party but the men who have to work under these principles believe this. The Public Service Alliance of Canada has stated clearly that it supports the idea of the resolution not being made into a statute, as does, too, the Professional Institute of Canada. Because the employees' groups do not support the Conservative amendment and because, as I have explained, it would mean rigidity instead of flexibility, our party will not support the Conservative motion.
The road to bilingualism in the country as a whole is a difficult one. But it is worth it. The road to bilingualism in the civil service is equally difficult but equally worth taking. It will take time, it will take tolerance and it will take understanding. But despite our quarrels and our frustrations, I believe Canadians are basically a tolerant people. Because of bilingualism we are a richer country. Indeed, the leader of our party pointed out the other day that if we did not have an official policy of bilingualism in this country we would not have a policy of multicultural-ism either. Together, both linguistic groups can build Canada for greater things. Together we can promote unity but still maintain our diversity.
Last January, Mr. Speaker, when I made my maiden speech, I devoted part of it to the issue of bilingualism. At that time I quoted the late Governor General Georges P. Vanier. I would like to do so again, because I think his words have much meaning for us in Canada when we talk about bilingualism and biculturalism. He gave this address on New Year's Eve, 1967, shortly before his death. He said:
The measure of our unity has been the measure of our success in the past. . .
If we imagine that we can now go our separate ways within our country, if we think that selfish interests can now take precedence over the national good, if we exaggerate our differences or revel in contention, if we do any of these things we will promote our own destruction.
26314-65J

June 4, 1973
Official Languages
Canada owes it to the world to remain united because no lesson is more badly needed than the one our unity can provide-the lesson that diversity need not be a cause for conflict, but, on the contrary may lead to richer and nobler living.
He went on:
Let us open the windows and doors of the provinces. Let us look over the walls and see what is on the other side. Let us know one another, and that will lead to understanding.
I pray God that we may all go forward hand in hand. We can't run the risk of this great country falling into pieces.
All I can say to that is: Amen.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most of the problems with which we deal in this House of Commons are political in the truest and best sense of the word. Honest differences underline most of our debates here in this chamber. This idea is, perhaps, central to the fundamental workings of our parliament. Sometimes I become slightly suspicious when members of parliament, individually or collectively, cry out for a bipartisan approach to this or that issue being discussed on the floor of this chamber.
Having said that, I am as sure of one thing as never before: if we as parliamentarians let this debate on bilingualism fall into the partisan political arena, the damage to Canada, and to this parliament as an institution, will be incalculable. In my view, this is no exaggeration. Call it a cliche, call it a motherhood statement, but I approach this debate today in a spirit of seriousness that I have approached no other debate in this House previously.

I am sure of one thing, Mr. Speaker. When-

speechtext: You should have spoken before the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).

speechtext: I beg your pardon.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: You should have spoken before the right hon. member for Prince Albert.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext: You should have spoken before Dief.

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Perhaps I should. But let me say to the hon. member that I do not think it is helpful when the hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Pelletier) calls us dinosaurs, or when Mr. Pickersgill says that all the bigots are on this side of the House. I hope the hon. member will contain himself and attempt to ascertain what I am trying to do in this debate.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure of one thing: it rests with each hon. member to see to it that politics is excluded from the debate on bilingualism.

With questions relating to national unity in the truest sense-bilingualism, multiculturalism and language rights-in spite of what I said at the opening of my remarks, special considerations surely exist which should invoke a bipartisan approach on the part of each and every

member of this House. I think most of us realize that this is the first time in the history of the western world that a country has attempted to, let us say, superimpose the parliamentary system on a young federal union which at the same time is multicultural and has certain language rights, as we in Canada have today. Surely, this demands the highest kind of leadership and statesmanship by each and every member of this House. If I sound as though I am preaching a little, I make no apologies. The question of language rights in a young federal union such as Canada should never become the subject matter of partisan political debate, and in this regard I underline again and again the leadership role expected of us in this regard by every Canadian.
If I may digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, if I deal with general propositions in this House today it is because I deeply feel and believe that they are propositions that must be discussed before we give this resolution, or a bill or amended bill, our approval and clause by clause consideration. All four parties in this House must approach this subject as national parties. To do otherwise would be to abandon the trust that, in my view, the Canadian people have placed in our hands.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, as this debate goes on with other hon. members in the House, I think-and this is not an overstatement-of Canada but also of my constituency of Brome-Missisquoi whose population is 70 per cent Frenchspeaking and 30 per cent English-speaking.
In my own riding, as well as in several other ridings, national unity exists in the true sense of the word. I will remember to my dying day that when I started my political life 15 years ago in Ottawa-I must admit it-I spoke broken French; it was even worse than now. I will remember to my dying day the warm and courteous welcome I received from my constituents, my French-speaking fellow citizens. Like the previous speakers, I have pleasant memories of my first years in Ottawa.
For example, a French-speaking constituent from Farn-ham in my riding wanted to tender with the Department of National Defence. Immediately after I received his request on the phone and then his letter, the papers from the Public Service in Ottawa arrived at my office written entirely in English. My constituent had to submit his tender within three or four days, and the officials here in Ottawa told me: Mr. Grafftey, you have to wait three or four weeks for a French translation. Mr. Speaker, I found that quite ridiculous 15 years ago, and I hope I finally settled the matter not through an act of Parliament or a regulation, but with a simple phone call.
Let us look now at the other side of the picture, Mr. Speaker. Unfortunately, I am aware of what is going on today, and I do not want, as I said earlier, to make a political issue out of this question, but I remember something that happened a few weeks ago with regard to the government of the province of Quebec. Unfortunately, as I said a while ago-the population is 30 per cent Englishspeaking in Brome-Missisquoi-too often I write in English to my fellow citizens and to the provincial government and too often I receive letters written entirely in French. That is the opposite of what was happening 15 years ago in Ottawa.

There is one thing I want to make quite clear, Mr. Speaker: As a Canadian, not as a Tory in the Progressive Conservative party, I am going to fight to the last to secure the same language rights for my French-speaking fellow-countrymen throughout Canada, as I have always done for English-speaking Quebecers. One must respect the same language rights and grant the same protection to Anglophones and Francophones.
Let us put our cards on the table right now, Mr. Speaker. In my constituency of Brome-Missisquoi we have bigots on both sides of the picture. But, Sir, I am sure of one thing: I have no mandate from anybody in my riding to give them the time of day in this House of Commons. I, along with every other member of this House, have no mandate either-and I repeat this time and time again-to allow the issue of bilingualism to become a partisan political issue. The mandate I do have in this debate and in this House of Commons is to reach out across the floor of this House, and to my left in this chamber, to unite Canada- not as a Progressive Conservative, but as a Canadian first.
Only when we work as Canadians first to settle this question, in the spirit of the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) who spoke so well last Friday in this chamber, only in that spirit-especially those of us of the contemporary generation; and I do not say that in respect of any difference in chronological age but, rather, in respect of those especially who perhaps view national unity in a contemporary, outgoing way-and only by adopting this attitude and acting as Canadians first and settling this issue once and for all, can we get on with the real and true task of nation-building.
However, I must say that in my view the present parliament has a very special obligation toward the people of Canada in relation to language rights. Let us put our cards on the table now and briefly and objectively state what they are. I fully realize I am only one of two members in my party from the province of Quebec. At the same time, Sir, within my party there is great strength and representation from western Canada where the creative and positive forces of multiculturalism are so often and so well expressed. Partisan debate in the past on the subject of language rights has given far too many Canadians the feeling of having been left out and ignored in what should be a non-partisan, family debate. There is no use mincing words: this approach that has been followed in the past must stop, and stop immediately.
At this point I should like to speak very frankly-I am not exchanging accusations across the floor of this House-with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) about an important consideration which in my view touches both directly and indirectly on any discussion of language rights.

-language rights in general or language rights in the Public Service of Canada, Mr. Speaker.
Since he came to Ottawa, the hon. Minister of Transport pointed out on many occasions that the Progressive Conservative party is not a national party. I regret Mr. Speaker that my party has only two members from Quebec in
Official Languages
the House of Commons, but I am sure the hon. Minister of Transport also regrets to see only one Liberal member in Alberta.

The fact is that both the Minister of Transport and myself are members of great national parties. To say otherwise is to play partisan politics with the very fabric of national unity. I well remember the time between 1958 and 1962 when the Liberal opposition of the day was not much more than a corporals' guard in this House of Commons, with more than half their members coming from the province of Quebec. Was it ever suggested in the press, or was it ever suggested from this side of the House of Commons that it had ceased to be a national party? The answer definitely is no, it was never suggested.
If the Minister of Transport persists in the theory that only his party is the party of national unity, or the indispensable force for Canadian unity, the result would be catastrophic: it would mean that the only political parties which Quebec citizens, or Canadians living in the province of Quebec would have would be the Liberal party or the Parti Quebecois. We all know what that would mean eventually.

Anyway, I remain ever convinced of the common sense of the Canadian population in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces.

While I have never agreed with the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) interpretation of the constitution, especially as it affects federal-provincial relations, I have never attacked his federalist credentials either within or outside this chamber, nor have I ever suggested since my entry into political life that his party has ceased or will cease to be a national party. I ask members opposite, including the Minister of Transport, to re-examine their theories concerning what is and what is not a national party at the present time.
Sir, in relation to the question of bilingualism I repeat that this Parliament has an awesome responsibility. Primarily, we must not confuse language rights with cultural rights and cultural identity. I was particularly impressed by some of the remarks of the Prime Minister when he opened the debate on this resolution. He said that whatever the historical facts vis-a-vis language rights were in 1867, 100 years ago, 100 years later we are faced with other political and social considerations.
What are these? I have already alluded to them. The first thing that comes to my mind is that the vast majority of members from my province find themselves sitting on the government side of the House, while the vast majority of members representing the dynamic, creative forces of multiculturalism sit with my party on this side of the House and, I should say, with the NDP, the hon. members to my left. Need I say any more? Surely, these facts alone call for the highest kind of statesmanship to be practised by all parties and all hon. members in this domain. The Canadian people expect nothing less from us. They have given us a mandate to play our part in uniting Canada.

June 4, 1973
Official Languages
It must be admitted, Mr. Speaker, that I have some difficulty to follow the speech of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).

I repeat that it is with some trepidation, and at the risk of sounding somewhat presumptuous, that I wish to address a few words especially to the Prime Minister. Considering the fact that he feels this resolution standing in his name to be so important, and he had so much to say about it-I have never said this before, but at least I think I know some of the awesome responsibilities that a prime minister must shoulder-and in view of the importance which most hon. members attach to this debate, it is regrettable that he has not seen fit to be present in the House.
