speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
However, I wish to address a few words especially to him as prime minister of my country, my prime minister, and to the prime minister of another day, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).
The Prime Minister came to office not only with a national mandate but with a special knowledge of the political forces at play in his native province in the late 1960s. He came to make Ottawa a meaningful capital and to make federal Canada a viable option for millions of Canadians living in the province of Quebec. It constituted a large part of his mandate. Who, in all honesty, could question the sincerity of this mission? The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, the first prime minister of Canada with other than French or British origin as he said today, gave with pride particular expression to the forces of multiculturalism so often-as we have heard and as we are going to hear in the House-to be found within the context of western Canada.
I do not think I will be giving away any caucus secrets when I say that in 1962 and 1963, both inside and outside our caucus the right hon. member for Prince Albert, who was then prime minister, had articulated his desire for an all-party conference which would be non-partisan in nature and which would involve legislators from all parties at all levels of government, and Canadians other than legislators from many walks of life. Such a great conference was to update many constitutional considerations, such as language rights and the rest, as we approached our centennial. I, frankly, think that the fact it was never held is to be regretted. I do not know what kind of progress we would have made, but the fact it was never held is to be regretted.

But unfortunately, since 1962-and I do not want to throw all the blame on one party or another, because both sides are perhaps responsible and as far as I am concerned maybe I would accept the blame-the matter of language rights has too often been mixed up with politics.


As I said at the outset that if we continue to do this only Canada and only this institution of Parliament will suffer because we will not be getting on with the real and fundamental issues of nation-building.
Past misunderstandings and wounds must be buried and forgotten. Members on both sides of the House have awesome responsibilities in this regard. If there is currently misunderstanding between the positive Canadianism to be found in the French fact and the positive pride in Canadianism to be found in the creative forces of multiculturalism, I plead with the two right hon. gentlemen in the House to show imagination and leadership, as I know they can, to lessen the suspicion and misunderstanding. I plead with the present prime minister and the past prime minister. Everyone knows what I am talking about here. It could be argued that both of them lost working majorities because of misunderstanding in this regard. I do not believe that, but there is perhaps misunderstanding, bitterness and suspicion in this respect. I plead, as I have never pleaded with the House before, for those two right hon. gentlemen to show what I know is their capacity for leadership and imagination and to water down the suspicion and misunderstanding that exists.
People like ourselves who have seen national unity work, where the English and the French work side by side, such as in my little village, might find it very difficult to emphasize with this misunderstanding and suspicion. But it does exist somewhere, and surely national leadership by both the present and the past prime minister is something that younger, contemporary-thinking members of this House may ask for if we are to have a decent Canada in which to live.
There is a common denominator of pride in Canada to be found in the French fact and in the multicultural mosaic. Every time I travel west I sense this pride in Canada in the west, as in all other parts of Canada. Both sides of the House owe it to Canada and to Canadians to join forces to strengthen this common bond of feeling.
I plead as I have never pleaded before that this House accept the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). Why the resolution was put forward in the first place, not as an amendment to the Official Languages Act but in this form, escapes me. I say this without any partisan intentions whatsoever. It seems to me that if what I hear in the House is correct, by voting for the amendment we will allay those fears, perhaps unjustified, that this resolution was purely a political ploy.
Members on the government side have stated that we should have enough flexibility to permit change as the situation evolves. What kind of change? What kind of flexibility? Change by administrative decree and ordinance that has already created confusion and misunderstanding? Change in the intention of this resolution without reference to parliament? That is just what we shall have if the resolution before the House is not amended so that its provisions become an amendment to the Official Languages Act.
I say to members of all parties, as a first act in climbing onto bipartisan ground: For the good of Canada, accept this amendment. We are not trying to shove it down
June 4, 1973

anyone's throat. It might not be the be all and end all, but surely the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) knows what I mean when I say, and will continue to say: For the good of Canada, accept this amendment. There is no trickery involved.
My leader is in the House, and I say that if there was one reason he came into national politics it was to play his part in uniting this country. Do hon. members think he put the amendment forward as political trickery? No. You can read between the lines when I say: In the name of Canada, accept this amendment and take this issue out of the political arena once and for all. It would be the first act we could all do together as we climbed onto bipartisan ground, without accusing each other and pointing to where the bigots are. Who knows where they are? Let us not give them the time of day in this place, Mr. Speaker.
If future changes are needed, let parliament, in good faith, do the amending. No resolution, be it ever so pious, will serve us well. Matters of this import cannot be left to administrative whim: surely we have learned that lesson. For some years now the Official Languages Act has been administered without real reference to parliament. The results, no matter what we feel they should be, are far from satisfactory. They are there for all to see. Surely government members have come to distrust a purely administrative approach to directing language matters.
Parliament must be consulted when basic changes are involved. Is there any doubt about that, when this is something that goes to the very fabric of our national unity? I have seen too many agencies of government, including Radio Canada, fly in the teeth of resolutions which had all-party support. Sir, this resolution must become an amendment to the Official Languages Act. I ask members of the party opposite to get hold of the Prime Minister tonight, have him join hands with my leader, and in a spirit of bipartisanship accept this amendment once and for all.

But we would have several things to add particularly if my proposals have been considered seriously. But, Mr. Speaker, it is not necessarily in the House of Commons- even with a piece of legislation or an amendment-that are settled matters concerning linguistic rights within the Public Service of Canada or even outside, without a true sense of understanding and goodwill and, I am sure that most members are such minded. But, Mr. Speaker, provinces must also play their part as far as the teaching of a second language is concerned.

I suppose we all know that we can do what we want by fooling around with acts, by amending acts, by looking at clauses and subclauses. But we will only succeed if there is a positive spirit of good will as we approach this subject. I am glad somebody is extremely sincere and progressive in his attitude to this problem; I refer to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). We have had many private conversations. I know he shares my view that the provinces can fulfil a much stronger role in teaching a second language, and if they do our job of uniting the country will be made somewhat easier. I feel that many of the programs he has
Official Languages
initiated will help in this regard. I can do nothing but encourage him and give him support from this side of the House. We should implore the provinces to do this, not only the province of Quebec but our other provinces. [Translation]
-to improve what is being done, Mr. Speaker, to that effect.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me simply state that we do not know our strength if we do not know our history. Confederation was an act of faith. Liberals and Conservatives joined hands to bring Canada and Canadians together. There was no indispensable man; there was no indispensable party. The Fathers of Confederation acted as Canadians first. Confederation was an act of national unity; there was no room for partisan debate.
Today, over 100 years later, a few things have changed. We now have four parties represented in a minority situation in the House of Commons. Millions of people have since come to Canada from many lands other than the United Kingdom and France, a fact which the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert articulated so well today. Yet, Sir, one thing has not changed; that is the necessity for each Member of Parliament to adopt the spirit of the Fathers of Confederation as we discuss the question of language rights.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we members are often accused of talking in the House to our constituents. Today I am addressing myself to every Canadian of English mother tongue. I am using the other official language to speak to you to emphasize the instant translation facilities available to us here in Ottawa and that these remarks will appear in Hansard, printed in both official languages. Easy communication is maintained though the majority of the English mother tongue members of this House have little or no fluency in their country's other language.
This last statement is not a criticism. We must accept as a well illustrated truth, that persons that have passed the half way point in their lives are not likely to have either the ability or the desire to become fluent in another language.

June 4, 1973
Official Languages
Very few persons are fortunate enough to live in bilingual households. Outside the province of Quebec there is only a negligable amount of business that is not conducted in the English language. In nine provinces, the opportunity rarely exists where a person can be immersed in a French-speaking environment.
We must also realize in our assessment of our current situation that the standard of second language instruction across the country leaves much to be desired. Far less attention has been paid to language instruction than other subjects. In many countries of Europe, a second language rates equally with other school subjects and a pass mark is a prerequisite for graduation.
In Canada, whether we be of English or French mother tongue, we have tended to build a resistance to school instruction in the second language that has lowered teaching standards and encouraged antipathy in our young people. In a communication vaccum, people tend to become emotional and sometimes afraid. American visitors enjoy Quebec because of its French language and distinctive atmosphere. The same attitude is found in English speaking vacationers in Quebec. This enjoyment is enhanced by the realization that they will not be lost or embarrassed because they speak one language. The unilingual English person demands the right to the protection afforded by the use of his or her own language. Why, then, is there English resistance to the establishment of minimal rights for unilingual French-speaking persons? Why is this motion necessary when we already have the Official Languages Act?
As it states in the initial paragraphs of the motion, it is necessary to recognize and approve the principles for the achievement of the objectives of the Official Languages Act.
Separatism is not unique to the province of Quebec. Here in this capital city, groups actively work for a unilingual English-speaking Canada. Many English-speaking persons refuse to accept the way of life of several millions of their fellow Canadians. This English separatism is just as deadly as the French variety, just as short sighted, just as bigoted and just as detrimental to the future prosperity and well being of every citizen of this country.
What then are we asking? Not that all English speak French, not that all the French speak English. But only that anyone communicating with their federal government be at ease and easily understood in the official language of their choice. That a unilingual French person have an opportunity to work for his government in his own language. That is all.
I am not going to repeat lengthy statistics. The inbalance is abundently self evident: 3.6 per cent of the appointments to the public service in 1971 were unilingual French. 81.7 per cent were unilingual English.
The last paragraph in the motion before us deals with the National Capital region and the desire to enhance its bilingual character. We have a long way to go. Here, at the Parliament of Canada it should hardly be necessary to stress that visitors should be able to address all officials in either of our official languages.
(Mr. Herbert.]
That this condition does not exist one hundred and six years after the birth of our nation is no credit to this House.
Language was a factor in the last election and no discussion of degree will alter that fact. It is an unfortunate truism that many persons will say one thing and do another. This is a particular weakness amongst politicians.
I am appealing to you as men and women who fight for Indian rights, for Eskimo rights, for the right to worship God in your own way and as men and women who respect the rights of others in a free society. I am not worried about the vote on this motion. I am concerned about our individual actions today and tomorrow.
To members who stress the merits of the official languages act, but suggest that we are moving too fast, I would ask to change sides just long enough to face the reality of the situation as it exists today.
Those of you that actively support Indian rights have cultivated an appreciation of the different way of life of the Indian.
Our two official languages also represent two different ways of life. A recognition of that fact will put an end to fence sitting.
If you have to wrestle with your conscience, before you recognize the right to equality of service and opportunity of our French language citizens, then I suggest that voter consideration is overriding human consideration.
I am extremely fortunate in being able to enjoy each day our very special Canadian way of life. Let us all actively work to improve it.

Mr. Speaker, during the course of this debate we have heard a great deal of important rhetoric which I could not hope to emulate in speaking of the involvement of this question of language in the whole concept of national unity in our country. I say at the outset that I would not quarrel with anyone who says that the issue is an important one from the point of view of the future of our country and the relationship between our two great races which just over 100 years ago started as a partnership to develop a nation through agreement, understanding and compromise. I want to put my position with respect to this resolution in a somewhat different light from the positions which have been expressed thus far in this debate.
Although the debate seems to have centered on national unity, I want to remind all my colleagues in this House of certain facts. I ask the government not to forget that there is a very important human element involved in this debate. Thousands of public servants, the majority of whom live in the national capital area, have their eyes on the actions of this government and their ears on the debate taking place in parliament. So I rise to speak in this debate, Mr. Speaker, conscious that I have the honour to represent in parliament a large number of public servants and their families who at one time or another have been bumped and buffeted and have found themselves in the eye of what I said on a previous occasion was a
June 4, 1973

"bilingual hurricane". It is to this aspect of the matter that I wish to address myself.
I have found that for public servants the issue is not the Official Languages Act as such. The act was debated and its principles were examined by another parliament. The result of the examination was that all parties in the House at that time endorsed the principles of the Official Languages Act. For those public servants to whom I have referred the big question is not the act; the question is, what is the real and true intention of the government in advancing this resolution at this time?
I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) who represents my neighbouring riding, Ottawa-Carleton, and who represents, as I do, a large number of public servants. He said this afternoon that the purpose of the resolution is not to reopen an old debate. One could be forgiven if one doubted that, in view of the utterances made in this House. I say that we should close the debate. The minister said that the purpose of the resolution is to review the principles under which the act is to be applied and under which implementation of the program is to take place in the public service.
Mr. Speaker, I think this question goes far beyond a mere matter of review. I think it comes down to this: we must enshrine within the law of this country certain principles which are designed to protect the interests of public servants, particularly unilingual public servants, in every part of Canada. The minister said the purpose of this resolution is to undercut the arguments of separatism. I say that we should go further and this House should make a pronouncement that will pull the rug from under the separatist element in this country.
When I have spoken to public servants about this matter, they have reminded me that this is the same government that has refused consistently to bring forth long overdue amendments to the Public Service Employment Act with respect to broadening the bargaining rights of public servants. This is the same government, Mr. Speaker, that has paid lip service to the principle of full escalation of public service pensions, a principle which we support, but has used what I call shabby legal arguments to avoid bringing the question before this House. This government has not taken in these areas any steps which are really meaningful to public servants.
Is it any wonder that public servants view with skepticism the resolution before the House? I hasten to add they are not skeptical about the words they read; their skepticism is centred around the real intention of this government. They are asking me and others how there can be any assurance that the important nine points now enunciated, and so long overdue, will have an effect on the day to day operations of the Public Service of Canada and will continue to have such an effect in the offices of individual public servants.
The fact is, as has been stated before, that this government has dangerously neglected to give the Canadian public a candid and comprehensive explanation of the Official Languages Act and their bilingual policy. They have failed to explain to Canadians, particularly public servants, in down to earth, practical terms the real mean-
Official Languages
ing of the statute and that which flows from it. There is no doubt that whatever steps they have failed to take, must be taken now so that misunderstandings can be corrected, so that misinterpretations that exist in the national capital can be eliminated, and so that all Canadians, not just public servants, will understand the true effect and meaning of the statute and the government's policy.
I met thousands of public servants in the fall of 1972. I say to this House, it is to their everlasting credit that the public servants of Canada generally supported the principles of the Official Languages Act.

That was their position. They recognized that the purpose of the act was to give equal status in the public service and in the Government of Canada to the two official languages. The act states that the two languages-
-shall possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the Parliament and Government of Canada.
Parliament enacted that statute. The government that brought it forward was vested with the duty to ensure that every public servant, and those contemplating entry into the public service, should possess and enjoy equality of status. It is, therefore, the duty of all members of this House, particularly those on the government side, to ensure that in the process of implementating the bilingual program in the public service, equality is assured for all public servants.
The problem is very serious. If we can solve the problems of the public servants employed during this period of transition, a period when we are trying to remake 105 years of history within a relatively short time, we will have gone a long way toward fostering and promoting the spirit of the legislation and the principles set forth in the Official Languages Act.
I have said before, and I say again, that the policy of bilingualism means that within the limits of practicability Canadians should have the right to federal government service in either official language. We should continue to search for equality. There ought to be a commitment to equality. We must not forget that entering the public service and advancing within it must be based on equality of opportunity for all Canadians. Every Member of Parliament has a duty to ensure that the public service is a place where Canadians can work together. All members, not just those who represent public service ridings, must ensure that the public service is a place where justice is not only done to every public servant but where it is seen to be done.
We must never forget that bilingualism involves the right to be unilingual, and that that right applies to both English- and French-speaking Canadians. There was on this government a very heavy burden with regard to the public service of Canada. It is a matter of history and record that this government failed with respect to that burden.

the well-intentioned statement of a former prime minister now deceased will not be butteressed by anything which offers protection to public servants. Moreover, it is no argument to say that this amendment is right and proper and then to avoid it by suggesting that to embody protection in the law would cause inflexibility. The argument advanced against the amendment by my neighbour the Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton who represents a public service constituency, can only be described-I say this with regret

as the shabbiest legalism I have yet heard in the House of Commons. I join my leader in all the suggestions he made to improve the lot of public servants. I intend to vote for the resolution, but I would much prefer to be joined in an overwhelming vote for the amendment. I realize that two ministers of the Crown have taken a position against the amendment we have put forward, and that in the minds of some hon. members this may be a hurdle over which they feel they cannot vault. I do not want to go out on the campaign trail again and encounter that sort of atmosphere. I would much prefer to meet happy public servants than discontented ones. I ask the government to set the record straight so that every public

servant or prospective public servant, no matter from what part of the country he comes, can look upon the public service as a place for advancement, a service in which he feels trust, knowing that in his employment he is protected by the law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, invited to give my opinion on the resolution concerning the application of bilingualism within the civil service, I will certainly take this opportunity to express my views and, perhaps also, allay the anxieties of some hon. members who consider that the subject is raised much too often in the House.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, this resolution concerns a highly political subject which virtually affects the future of the whole Canadian people, and the members of all parties are certainly not wasting the time of the House when they publicly proclaim their opinion on one of the official languages in Canada.
We have adopted the Official Languages Act which was supported by most hon. members, by all party leaders and, of course, by all liberal members. In fact, not to admit it would be lying to one's self.
Moreover, over the past years, several interpretations have been made of the Official Languages Act and particularly of the respective roles that the French and English languages should play within the public service. Let us not deny it: Some fears have been expressed by many citizens and maybe also certain views were circulated through the public service which had nothing to do with reality.
Of course, the principles of the resolution may seem elementary but in view of the past confusion I think it is important to repeat these principles and to allow the most important political body of this country, namely the House of Commons, to state its position on those principles so that those responsible for the public administration may implement them with the knowledge that they have the Commons' confidence. Finally, basic principles will be implemented within the public service towards the essential objective which is to communicate in the language of one's choice at all federal levels.
I think I can make this statement without anyone being able to charge this government with politicking on bilingualism and, on the other hand, without charging the other hon. members and mainly the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) or the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) to try and play politics with this debate, which is basic if we are to understand that in the public service there exists a system by which opportunities and chances are equal for all Canadians. And I am rather convinced that the application of this resolution can better serve the causes of French- than English-speaking people because in the past, a certain group of French Canadians have rather been disinterested towards the federal public service, for reasons that can very easily be understood. There is also something that could be called not discrimination but a tendency to place people on a side line, because it is easier to understand each other when you are using the same language; it is also normal to deal
Official Languages
with an assistant, a helper speaking your own language, because that very important vehicle is essential to communicate with human beings.
Generally speaking, I think that this confirmation of principles by the House of Commons is timely; Mr. Speaker, if the resolution accepted by the House had no result other than to clear up the confusion in the mind of a number of civil servants and if the population could understand that we are trying to provide all Canadians with basic services they are entitled to when we are talking about the language of communication, either French or English, we would have reached an important point and at the same time, we would have insured better understanding between all Canadians be they from Vancouver, Quebec or the Maritimes.
Mr. Speaker, I think I am right when I say, without claiming that Canada is the country which is doing most for the French language, that we must realize that we are the most privileged persons in the world with the best means of communication to be able to use equally English or French which are both world wide communication languages. We must take better advantage of that asset in the federal public service where some gaps still remain to be filled. It is important and imperative for the government and for the House of Commons, because it it the higher political body in the country, to provide guidelines for those who will have the responsibility to apply them in order to ensure services in both official languages.
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that our country is one of the most privileged countries because it has the opportunity to enjoy both English and French, which are two universal languages. Furthermore, with our means of communication, radio and television for instance, we are perhaps the country which contributes the most for the progress of both languages and particularly French, because I think that French-speaking Canadians, those who have a French Canadian origin in Canada, have a right to wonder.
All hon. members who speak French are members of an international association of parliamentarians. In 1971 we had the pleasure and good fortune of welcoming the representatives of 28 states. They were parliamentarians of French-speaking countries. I think, Mr. Speaker, that these natural relations between states, through the vehicle of thought which is language, are a considerable enrichment.
I think there is no need to recall that at the United Nations as well French is one of the official languages of communication.
But in a country like ours, Mr. Speaker, where a third of the population speaks French and where important steps have been taken by youth to learn one of the official languages a considerable improvement took place these last few years. I think it is important that hon. members make a decision on this question and state openly that some positions must be recognized as essentially bilingual to ensure the citizen the possibility of communicating in the language of his choice when dealing with the government.
One can say of course, once again, that it is elementary; previous years have shown that we had to come back to the subject, talk about it again and that the House of

June 4, 1973
Official Languages
Commons has to make a decision on the matter. If most hon. members can accept this essential point, we will have taken a giant step forward or we will have accomplished significant progress towards national unity, towards well understood Canadian unity and we will have ensured the basic elements of a healthier understanding between Canadians, whatever their province.
I have received open letters and I know quite well that it is the same for several other members. Frankly, I cannot understand how Canadians can now speak of a possible unilingual country, of having one single language and one culture. These people, however, make an effort to write in excellent English. Yet, I believe that these people are not dishonest, but they really lack information. And perhaps their leaders have failed to fulfill the duty incumbent upon them, that is to describe really the nature of our country, how it was constituted, and finally, that there were at least six million French-speaking people in Canada and that bilingualism was not too important in some parts of our country.
I know that in my riding, 99.9 per cent of the people speak French; speaking bilingualism has some importance because it opens the doors of the public service to Frenchspeaking people, which was very difficult in the past since there was some reluctance to do it. To be able to understand and speak to one another, I think that this is one of the most important aspects of the resolution now before us, which recognizes that public servants should be able, under the provisions of the Official Languages Act, to fulfill their duties within the government in the official language of their choice.
I come back to the theme of the resolution which, in a country which was established in 1867, must be considered by people like me as entirely elementary. But, in my opinion, it had to be said in order to secure a better understanding and give public servants who will be responsible for the implementation of these principles the authority to ensure, once and for all, that the individual who will write a letter in French will be able to get an answer in French and that he who will write in English will get an answer in English.
Mr. Speaker, in closing I will say a few words concerning those who maintain that those administrative criteria should be incorporated in the Official Languages Act. Administrative criteria, or principles, which are somehow the guidelines in the implementation of the Official Languages Act in the public service, could very well be called regulations.
But regulations are not part of the legislation, and to answer the hon. member who proceded me, I will simply state that he does not have to get impatient, that if the House agrees to that motion, as I have a feeling it will, the government, which has always moved forward in the implementation of a genuine policy on bilingualism, both within the public service and in connection with the official languages and all the federal institutions, is still really the one which can offer the greatest possible pledge that the rights of individuals will be respected. It will however be necessary to make sure that the language of the citizen can be used as a basis and can likewise be used

in the public service, and that the official positions will be duly filled.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, when the Leader of the Opposition suggests or recommends that that resolution be made an integral part of the Official Languages Act, I for one do not question his sincerity.
However, at the political level-it may be a very clever suggestion or proposal-I would like to suggest to him that he will have to secure the support of the majority or the totality of the members of his party. The Leader of the Official Opposition is one of the leaders-and I say this with a very open mind, Mr. Speaker-who for the first time as leader of the Progressive Conservative party really sets himself on basic issues at the level of a head of a national party.
However, Mr. Speaker, that is a lot. I know that the House gave him an ovation when he rose to officially support the Official Languages Act against the will of a group of members of his party. He showed real courage.
I lr. Speaker, to those members who are concerned about the fact that this issue comes back very often before the House, I merely say that when voluntarily and with good faith those criteria will be allowed to be applied and become the policy followed within the public service, that is a question which will disappear at the national level and at the same time we will have set the cornerstone to really ensure a well-understood national unity among all Canadians for they will be able to talk to and understand each other.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I should like to emphasize very strongly that I have never quarrelled with the provisions and the spirit of the Official Languages Act. In my view, the problems which have arisen in this country in connection with bilingualism are the direct result of the methods this government has used in the course of implementing that act.
It is my opinion that the government has followed a path filled with unnecessary and unfair actions which scarcely do anything but bring a sea of trouble following behind them. I find no reason to believe this situation would necessarily undergo any change for the better by the passage of the resolution now before this House. Indeed, I believe this government has performed a great disservice to the cause of Canadian unity by pursuing policies of confrontation rather than policies of co-operation in respect of its method of instituting bilingualism in Canada.
I do not hesitate to say there are those who have been, and still are, dividing this country by using the issue of bilingualism for political purposes. Indeed, they have been using the whole subject of national unity for political purposes. The people doing that most certainly are not sitting on this side of the House.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
Since the passage of the Official Languages Act I believe it has become quite clear that the government has hoped to characterize probably all Canadians
June 4, 1973

into two basic groups in so far as attitude toward bilingualism is concerned. The first category is composed of all those who agree with every single thing this government has done in connection with the implementation of the bilingual program. It is almost as if we are expected to believe these are the only people who stand for national unity and that these are the people who are good Canadians because they are prepared to accept without question the supposed rightness of the government's bilingual policies.
In the second category I believe the government has sought to place all persons who would in any way whatsoever criticize or find any fault in respect of the methods of instituting bilingualism. These, therefore, are the people who are against national unity and are the bad Canadians because they are the people who have committed the supposedly shocking crime of being unwilling to accept without question the divine rightness of the government's method of instituting bilingualism in this country.
I submit, however, there is a third category of people in this country which this government has conveniently overlooked. I suggest it is the largest category of Canadians by far. It is composed of thousands and thousands of people across the land who have never quarrelled with the principles of bilingualism but who have been shocked and utterly appalled at the methods used by this government to institute its bilingual program. This third group is made up of Canadians who love their country too much to allow it to be torn apart by a government that has been, and is, playing politics with bilingualism and national unity, a government that gives unctuous lip service to national unity while at the same time indulging in actions and following methods that, in short, will do more to disunite this country than even avowed separatists could hope to accomplish. And, with regret, I suggest that the motives behind the presentation of this resolution do not improve the situation at all; but I will come to that aspect of the matter a little later in my remarks.
This resolution is not legislation. It is not an amendment to the Official Languages Act. It is merely a resolution of this House which, if passed, might well not last beyond the life of this parliament. In short, it means no more than the "Pearson pledge". It is an exercise in futility. Why should we pass a resolution which would have no validity in law?
If this government was really sincere, if it was doing anything more than playing politics with this most important and most serious subject, if this government really wanted such guarantees and assurances to public servants to mean something of real substance, then it would have proposed without hesitation that the contents of this resolution be written into the Official Languages Act in the form of an amendment. But this it did not do. It remained for the leader of this party to move such an amendment.

speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: DECLARATION OF CERTAIN PRINCIPLES RESPECTING EMPLOYMENT IN PUBLIC SERVICE OF CANADA
speechtext:
I find such actions by this government contemptible, to say the least. But no one should find this government's actions surprising. When we look back to the throne speech debate in the early days of this session, and when we recall some of the remarks made at that time by the Prime Minister, we can only conclude that we were being given a preview of the kind of thinking that lies behind the drafting of this resolution. Indeed, at that time in the Prime Minister's ill-tempered remarks we were being provided with a setting of the stage for what was to come and for what is now before us for consideration. This resolution, in reality, is worthless because it will have no legal validity, because its life expectancy would be very limited if passed. We should well be asking ourselves why this House is being put through this whole exercise.
The preamble of this resolution is more or less a reaffirmation of the principles of the Official Languages Act. Is it necessary to reaffirm by resolution an act that is already the law of this land? What kind of nonsense is this? If the sun is shining on Parliament Hill, should this House be called together for purposes of passing a resolution that the sun is really shining? Is it necessary that parliament should consider pious, periodic reaffirmations of all legislation that passes? Why do we not have resolutions reaffirming the importance of old age security? Surely, we should rush right away into immediate consideration of a resolution reaffirming our belief in the value and importance of family allowances.
What else does this resolution contain other than pious reaffirmations? Supposedly, it sets forth certain guarantees for public servants. But we should ask ourselves; What does it really do? What does it really mean? For example, paragraph 3 of the resolution says that the knowledge of English and French is one of the elements of merit in the selection of candidates for bilingual positions. How on earth could this be otherwise? Would we fill a position requiring English and French with a person speaking Arabic and Afghan? The truth, I suggest, is very sad. It is a very sad truth indeed. This resolution is not at all what the government would have us believe it to be. It is, in reality, yet another example of how this government will play with the subject of bilingualism for political purposes.
Judging by the tone of his remarks on this subject in recent months, I believe it is obvious that the Prime Minister and the government wanted only one thing, namely, to introduce a motion on bilingualism that would divide the House, and therefore at the same time a motion that they hoped would enable them to sit back and say in effect, "Look at us; we are for national unity and the others are not. We alone can save this country." The unfortunate reality of it all is that the kind of twisted thinking that lies behind this resolution could ultimately destroy this country.
The government would have Canadians swallow the utter myth that only it is capable of maintaining national

June 4, 1973
Official Languages
unity. By this resolution, in my opinion, the government expected turmoil to be stirred up in this country, and then when the pot is nicely boiling the scenario calls for the Prime Minister and his associates to come riding in on their white horses, posing as the ones who will be the saviours of Canada as a nation from those who are painted as the advocates of disunity simply because we object to gross government errors in implementing bilingualism.
Some may say that the easiest way to put an end to such cheap melodrama on the part of this government would be to quietly vote for this resolution, to make no objections, to deny St. George his dragon, to leave this sick government tilting at its windmills. Perhaps that approach has some merit, but to follow it would make it necessary to vote for a farce-and this resolution is a farce, this government knows it is a farce, and it is essential that it be shown to Canadians for exactly what it is.
Mr. Speaker, if this government was really sincere we would not be faced with this resolution. We would have been faced, instead, at the outset with amendments to the Official Languages Act making specific guarantees to public servants the law of this land. Only, as I said previously and as I say again, the amendment proposed by the leader of this party would accomplish that fact.
But the government has shown by its past actions that it is not sincere on many things, particularly on the methods of implementing bilingualism. There has been ample time since the passing of the Official Languages Act to clearly illustrate this fact. If this government has failed to approach the subject of bilingualism according to the spirit of the Official Languages Act, according to the spirit and intention of the "Pearson pledge", is there any reason to believe now that this resolution will make things any different? I suggest there is no reason whatsoever.
Over the past few years the people of my riding have had the opportunity of witnessing at first hand the methods used by this government to implement bilingualism in Canada. We have very clearly seen the hypocrisy, the insincerity and the duplicity of the course followed by this government. The people in my constituency of Leeds saw the incredibly nonsensical and stupid actions of this government in attempting to create instant bilingualism at Canada Customs offices, with no regard for common sense, with no regard for unilingual public servants of long-standing or for the merit principle; in short, with complete disrespect for the so-called "Pearson pledge" in regard to the implementation of bilingualism. But that is a fantastic story in itself, filled with unfairness, filled with hypocrisy and, I regret to say, filled with downright dishonesty-a case well documented and completely provable in all its aspects and a case which I am prepared to stand upon firmly before any persons who wish to judge it impartially, anywhere and at any time.
At the height of the nonsense in my area I was president of the constituency Liberal association. At that time I received a letter which I believe describes the actions of the government very well indeed in regard to its methods of implementing bilingualism. The letter is dated March 2, 1970. I would like to read into the record this particular paragraph which it contains:

I am sure there are many cases of essentially good legislation being ruined by ham-handed implementation. This appears to be a good example.
That letter was written by Senator Richard J. Stanbury, president of the Liberal Party of Canada. Truer words were never written. I agree with Senator Stanbury's sentiments completely. But subsequently the ringmaster of the circus opposite cracked his whip and the trained seals all sprang into line.
Mr. Speaker, I hear questions from the opposite side of the chamber asking, "Who is your writer?" I am proud to say I write my own speeches, something which I do not think many members on that side do. The methods used by the government up until now to institute its bilingual program have been in many cases ill-conceived, thoughtless and unfair. In addition, the program has suffered greatly from the antics of that bumbling bureaucrat, John Carson, and from the ridiculous and foolish utterances of the Commissioner of Official Languages who flits hither and yon to his little soirees and tete-a-tetes mouthing such nonsense as "Westmount Rhodesians."
We must seriously ask ourselves these questions: If the government has failed in the past to implement fairly the Official Languages Act, is there any reason whatsoever to believe that things will be different in the future? And even if the substance of section 1 of the resolution is incorporated by amendment into the Official Languages Act, as the leader of this party has suggested, is there any reason to believe that the government will honour such provisions with sincerity-something it has utterly failed to show in the past toward implementation of the act itself? I am forced to conclude that anything the government does here and now is mere hollow window-dressing brought on by the near defeat of last October 30, and not in any way the result of a change of heart. Anything the government does now must be regarded as suspect against the background of its past actions.
Speaking in this House last Friday, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) said that he was amused at the amendment introduced by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and he tried to justify his amusement by going back to quotations from Hansard of 1969. But a lot has happened since 1969. Perhaps the most important lesson we have learned since 1969 is the fact that the record of the government in implementing bilingualism is such that the most definite and specific legal safeguards are required-required in order to be certain that bilingualism will be fairly and properly instituted in Canada for all concerned, required if for no other reason than the bumbling record of the government since 1969 in implementing bilingualism. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to expressing amusement I say to the Minister of Communications that there is nothing at all amusing about the government's record.
I do not believe it is exaggeration or inaccuracy to say that the government does not want an amendment to the Official Languages Act for a very good reason from its own point of view. That reason is not, as the Minister of Communications would have us believe, so that the government will be free to follow flexible guidelines to meet changing conditions. It is far more likely that the govern-
June 4, 1973

ment does not want an amendment because an amendment has legal permanency, whereas a resolution as proposed by the government, to put it charitably, can be easily modified or, to put it a little less charitably, easily ignored or disposed of. Many persons have discovered that their inevitable fate, when they disagree with the government on the methods of implementing bilingualism, is to be faced with an attempt to label them as bigots. This has been my own personal experience and I will not be surprised if it is my experience again after my remarks tonight.
But, Mr. Speaker, of French ancestry on both sides of my family, with a wife who comes from Holland, and as one who has always been an outspoken opponent of all forms of racism and bigotry, I totally reject such labels. I am proud that I can trace my ancestry back to Rene Cosset who came from the area of La Rochelle in France around 1700. I am equally proud of the fact, despite the childish and ridiculous interjections of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), that the French-speaking Cossettes of Quebec and the English-speaking Cossitts of Canada and the United States share a common ancestry that dates back several centuries to France.
If the government continues it past methods of implementing bilingualism-and those of us who have experienced these methods have no justification to expect it will do anything else-then I suggest that when the history of our age is written it will be said that this government destroyed national unity while it posed as its champion. It will be said that the sensible approach of co-operation between the English-and French-speaking peoples of this nation was forsaken for the senseless approach of confrontation. It will be said that this nation of Canada was torn apart by the policies of a government that played nothing but politics with bilingualism and national unity.

There is no suggestion that everyone in Canada must be bilingual as, unhappily, some have misinterpreted the meaning of the Official Languages Act. I believe it was the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) who last night indicated that a lot of Englishspeaking Canadians are of the opinion that most Quebeckers are bilingual because English-speaking Canadians have visited the metropolitan area of Montreal.
I can understand the frustration and the anger of the member for Champlain (Mr. Matte). He is well armed with statistics, and his statistics are honest. How do we change them, and how do we bring them more in line with the reality of Canada? The member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), when responding to the motion of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) concerning the status of women, indicated that his party might be prepared to accept the quota system in the interests of getting more women into senior levels of the civil service. I have not heard, however, whether this party would back the quota system in the interests of placing more people whose native tongue is French in the civil service.
The quota system is not fair, and I think it would be difficult to apply the quota system whether it is in the interests of placing more women in the civil service or more unilingual French-speaking Canadians. It is unfair to those already in place who have warranted promotion and who might be bypassed. It is not fair if the standards have to be lowered in the interest of implementing a quota

system. So we know the pitfalls of the quota system and we know that they are not fair.
We also know it is not fair that the proportion of French-speaking civil servants is so low. I can sympathize with the hon. member for Champlain. Can we do it by some words in debate, or applying a quota system? I do not know, but it is something we have to consider. Although I cannot accept all his views or arguments, I know that they stem from a deep-seated feeling shared by many of my French-speaking colleagues in the Liberal caucus.
When I am talking on this subject in my riding or other English-speaking parts of this country, I ask my audience to imagine for the moment that Queen Victoria, rather than naming Ottawa as the capital of Canada had selected, let us say Lac St. Jean where I understand the majority of people speak French, and beautiful French. Imagine if, with Lac St. Jean as the capital, on visiting your capital you heard only French spoken. Would you feel at home? Would you be frustrated if you were endeavouring to deal with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, finance, or external affairs only to find that there were very few people who could accommodate you in your own language? And how much greater would be the frustration if you were a unilingual, English-speaking Canadian!
That, then, is the dilemma and the problem faced by the French-speaking Canadian who comes to Ottawa and does not feel at home here. We have an obligation to make him feel at home in his country's capital. And where, as in my riding, there are pockets of French-speaking Canadians, I am pleased to see the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) making provision for grants so that the language and culture of the French-speaking Canadian can be preserved. I was pleased to note that over the past two years grants have been made to the Club Joliet in my riding. It was one of the highlights of my short political career to date that when addressing the club I was able to speak to them totally in French.
Some think it would be appropriate if I were to speak French in the present debate. If I were to do so, I would in my view miss the point of this particular debate. We are not saying to Canadians that they must speak two official languages; we are saying, "You can speak in your own tongue and express yourself in your own language." This is something I feel very strongly about. In any event, I feel it would be appropriate if I were to continue speaking in English rather than to demonstrate my halting French. In this exercise we are saying over and over again that every Canadian need not be bilingual. We are saying, however, that we are entitled to express our views in our own language.
I have had the privilege and I have enjoyed the opportunity of studying the French language since my election in 1968. It may be necessary for the Prime Minister and the government to use another phrase to describe my use of the French language-not functional, but possibly minifunctional. But what a challenge, Mr. Speaker, and how exciting it is to try a phrase and to realize that you have been understood; and how gratifying to realize that you can understand someone who is speaking French.

It is easier for me to learn French, thanks to the enthusiasm of my daughter Katie. I am proud she is making and has been making a determined effort to become, not functionally bilingual but bilingual. When my spirits sagged and I felt frustration or incapable of mastering the French language, my 14-year old daughter charged, shamed, encouraged and challenged me. I will continue to study, to practise, to listen and to speak French as my recognition of the French fact and acceptance of bilingualism in Canada. To those who are contemplating the study of French I would say, "Do it. There are many more rewards than there are frustrations, trials and tribulations."
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) asked in his remarks yesterday, "Why this resolution", and said it was not binding on the government. I say to the Leader of the Opposition that this resolution is put forward not only to show where the government stands but because the people of Canada must know where this parliament stands. It was encouraging to note that the Leader of the Opposition, speaking for his party, adopted and accepted the principles outlined. He would place them in legislation. I do not agree with that, because I think codifying these principles would make it extremely difficult to change them when changes should be made. I think there has to be some flexibility if there is to be fairness in the implementing of these principles. We are telling Canada and Canada's civil servants what will be the guiding principles in implementing the Official Languages Act in so far as they are concerned.
I compliment the Leader of the Opposition for the stand he has taken. I cannot argue too strongly against putting these principles into legislation. I think that might be too inflexible. He said he has received scars as a result of taking the stand he has taken. I say to him, they are honourable scars.

Mr. Speaker, I was one of those who originally supported the Official Languages Act, mainly because of the conciliatory action and direction of the late prime minister, Lester B. Pearson. At that time we were assured that this concept would not be implemented in such a way as to cause serious concern either to the civil service or to the people of Canada in general. Most of us who so voted believe, I think, that the proposals put forward in this resolution are the basis on which the Official Languages Act was passed. Therefore, I think few who voted originally for the Offical Languages Act would change their minds today.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) made a speech today that interested me, more because of what he said and interpreted than any facts he enunciated. He indicated that the proposals in this resolution were always in the mind of the government, and that the flexibility that all members on the government side are talking about as being necessary is at present a fact, because changes will continually be involved in this matter. He forgot to tell everyone that these nine points were brought before parliament in the form of a resolution because of the result of the election of last October.
It must interest people like Mr. Francis, Mr. Blair and certain other former Members of Parliament, particularly those from the Ottawa valley, to find this resolution

Official Languages
before us today, because as sure as I am standing here they were defeated for being unable to convince the government that it was necessary to provide the safeguards we are discussing in this resolution. It is interesting to note that several days after the election the government announced, through the medium of a statement by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), that civil servants were to be dealt with as this resolution proposes. It was to be directed in that direction.
For what happened in the past I fault not only the government but the civil service associations, and I include in that the professional associations. I fault, as well, the civil service and its agencies. Why? Because, Mr. Speaker, they were not able to solve some of the very simple problems which had arisen, and were not able to arrive at criteria that were acceptable either to the civil service authorities or to civil servants. I was therefore more impressed with the politics of this resolution than with the fact that parliament is being asked to endorse it. We are being asked to stand up and be counted again on a subject which we debated when the official languages bill was before the House.
As we are discussing this matter I think it behooves all members of the House to ascertain for themselves whether the flexibility that Liberal members are talking about is advantageous. I am of the opinion it is not advantageous. I am of the opinion that the principle put forward by Mr. Pearson and endorsed by most members of the House provided the civil service with a bill of rights which was to work in three ways. It protected those who were purely French-speaking in French communities; it protected those who were purely English-speaking in English communities, and it protected long-time civil servants who were in the never-never land in the middle, known as Ottawa.
The situation has not yet been resolved, for several good reasons. I come from an area where people are divided into several language groups. It includes French, English and many other nationalities. Approximately 30 to 35 per cent are French-speaking; the remainder are English-speaking. That district is to be designated under the act. Although the location of these bilingual districts has not been decided officially, in many instances such districts have been established. I use the example of Timmins. We had in Timmins for a number of years an acting postmaster. He was of Italian extraction, representing a large body of the population in Timmins. He also understood some English, having gone to school at his own expense. The Sisters in the community taught him some French. Therefore, he had some knowledge of three languages.
Because this is a bilingual district, although it has not yet been so designated, he was asked to appear before a board some two years after he had taken over as the acting postmaster in Timmins. When he appeared before the board the first question he was asked was whether he was bilingual. He said that he spoke English and had studied some French, although he was not fluent. I might say that although English has been his language for the past 35 or 40 years, he is not entirely fluent in that language either. He was told by the board, "If you are not bilingual, don't waste our time and we won't waste yours. Unless you are

bilingual there is no point carrying on this interview." It is this kind of situation that neither the civil service not the Civil Service Association have been able to correct. This has created many anomalies in the province of Quebec. On an opposition day the Creditiste party raised this matter on behalf of people they represent who are also faced with inequality of opportunity. The real desire of Canadians is a language bill of rights for those employed in the Public Service of Canada.
I do not support the amendment moved by the Conservative party, for a very simple reason. If it were accepted we would be here all summer amending every act because of the language problem. We would have to amend acts respecting the armed forces, the public service, Crown corporations and many others. I am not particularly interested in that exercise.
Earlier today I spoke to the President of the Treasury Board. There is no one more familiar with the operation of the public service than he. If he remains President of the Treasury Board I believe this resolution can be implemented as is. In my opinion it is good to have some flexibility so that the legislation can be changed from time to time. This is also true of the Bill of Rights. The right to privacy should be included in the Canadian Bill of Rights. It should provide the right to use either official language as well as religion or lack of religion.
We should be able to make changes to something we believe to be fundamental. The development of bilingual or unilingual units throughout the country is very fundamental to every Canadian. I was very interested in the speech this afternoon by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). It amused me. When I first came here 15 years ago there was no simultaneous translation system. When a member from Quebec made a speech in French everybody went out and had a smoke. No one listened and no one cared. The member making the speech did not care either because when he had completed his speech he went back to Montreal or Quebec City and we did not hear from him until he wanted to make another speech. Following the installation of the simultaneous translation system there was an obligation to consider every argument that was made. Other changes have been made which have been advantageous in the development of this country.
I am not sure whether we will go ahead holus-bolus with bilingual districts across Canada. I am not sure whether in communities where only English is spoken it will be necessary to have bilingual services. I hope that unilingual people in English communities will not be denied opportunities because the community in which they live is in a designated bilingual district. I am not sure this will be avoided, because it has already begun to some extent. We do not want to see anyone demoted because they cannot pass an examination. We must be very careful about how this policy is implemented. The resolution must not be totally ignored.
I think this government has done a lot of window-dressing. The member who preceded me said that he had been studying French since 1968, but he did not even give us a sample of what he has learned. Perhaps he does not require a second language in Sarnia. It may not do him any good. Perhaps he is engaged in an exercise of futility.

speechtext:
The classes lasted for two hours. After leaving a class to attend a committee meeting or a sitting of the House, you forgot all about French. You did not think of it again until you returned for another lesson two or three days later. Our teacher became very frustrated because it was necessary to start all over again. There is no way to learn a language or have any facility in it unless you speak it regularly. I am not very impressed with $45,000 a year deputy ministers who are able to answer one question per year in the second language. I suppose it cost $50,000 to train them. Who ran the shop while they were being trained? If an assistant deputy was running the shop, he should have had the job.
I suggest that to some extent this type of training is an exercise in futility. I am not opposed to everyone in this country being bilingual, and I am aware of some of the criticisms that members from the province of Quebec will make. I am prepared to vote reasonably large sums of money to create a bilingual nation. I am prepared to put that money into every kindergarten and primary school so that children may spend the first two or three years of their education totally within the climate of the other language.
Hon. members may wonder why this has not been done already. The reason is this, and my friends in the Social Credit party are well aware of it: a bilingual nation would quickly be created and the second generation would all be English-speaking, because on the North American continent English is the predominant language and, very likely, the second language would fall into disuse. If it fell into disuse and was no longer spoken in any normal business conduct, it would obviously no longer be accepted. I know that ability in the second language would make Canadians better people.
I am very proud that my father, my brother and other members of my family have always been able to speak French. I went to work at an early age and my job in the mines, apart from running the machines underground, was to train other people to speak the English language. That is why I murder it so badly-the result of the input from so many other languages! But I am very proud that my grandchildren speak French as their first language. I am sure they will grow up to be bilingual, because my son is not proficient in French.
These are all matters which will have to be considered carefully. The bigots on all sides must be convinced that the teaching of the second language is accompanied by very real rewards. I studied French in high school for four years. I was taught by a teacher who could not speak to any of the French people in the class or in the community. She went to Paris and learned a different type of French. It was like a person who had learned Latin trying to talk to Italians. She encountered a certain amount of difficulty.
Official Languages
In schools in Ontario the authorities usually hire a teacher who has a degree in the French language, rather than someone who can speak French. As a result, the time spent by the children is totally wasted.
Most members of this House are biased. Most members of this House and most people in the country are prejudiced. Nevertheless, there is a tradition in Canada of tolerance toward other people, of tolerance when we embark upon a program intended to produce a bilingual nation.I think there will be a great deal of tolerance shown on the part of parents. But you cannot give Ontario a large sum of money and tell them to run their education system on these lines because, obviously, they would find they were short somewhere else and would use the money for another purpose, as they are now doing.
If we are serious about language education, we shall need to arrange for exchanges of our people from different regions. If we decide to educate civil servants and they are willing to spend months at the task of learning the second language, then at least we should make sure they do this in Quebec rather than in Calgary or Ottawa.
If we are really considering the development of a bilingual policy in this country, we should be prepared to spend some money on it. It is for this reason I object to the resolution which has been placed before us, somewhat in the same terms as resolutions put forward when we want the Americans to get out of Viet Nam or when we want the French to discontinue exploding nuclear devices in the South Pacific in their atomic energy tests. The resolution should have been put into a form which would embody the controls which are being suggested in a way which it would be difficult to change. It seems that the resolution is an attempt to encourage the people of Quebec to believe they are part of this nation. Mr. Speaker, we decided that a long time ago. It has never been questioned in this House. Since I have been here I have not heard any member question whether the country should exist in the form in which it now exists.
What we are discussing is our lack of ability to produce the bilingual character which is necessary. I was very impressed when listening to the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) speaking recently in this debate. I was impressed by the fact that he moved a motion very similar in tone to the solution now before us. A spokesman for the government took objection to it and declined to support him. Now we see it in the form of a resolution-

subtopic: HARBOURS-ATLANTIC AREA-REQUEST FOR IMPROVED FACILITIES FOR FISHERMEN

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter C. Carter (St. John's West):
subtopic: HARBOURS-ATLANTIC AREA-REQUEST FOR IMPROVED FACILITIES FOR FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 15 I inquired of the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) about the provision of fishing and harbour facilities in the Atlantic area, particularly in Newfoundland and my riding of St. John's West. My question to the minister was prompted by the fact that in the Atlantic area, and in my riding in particular, there is a very desperate need for more and better harbour and fish landing facilities. I find that in my riding the Department of Public Works of the federal government is completely derelict in its responsibility to provide decent harbour and fish landing facilities to enable fishermen to successfully prosecute the fisheries.
The situation is not made any better when one realizes that this year the Department of Public Works has estimated its total expenditure on capital projects, maintenance and operation of public buildings to be $386,209,000. The situation is, of course, even further aggravated by the fact that in Ontario, where unemployment is around 4 per cent or 4.5 per cent, the expenditure on capital projects is $109,696,000. For maintenance work and operation of public buildings there is an expenditure of $96,484,000, or a total in the province of Ontario of $206,180,000.
In the Atlantic area, where we have an unemployment figure of 7.9 per cent, we find there is a capital expenditure of $15.5 million, with something like $12 million for maintenance and operation of public buildings. Of course, speaking for my own province, where we have an unemployment rate of 16.2 per cent, we find that on capital projects there is an expenditure of $4 million and something like $3.5 million for maintenance and operation of public buildings, for a total of $7,749,000. These figures were submitted recently to the Standing Committee on Public Works by officials of the Department of Public Works, and substantiated by the Department of the Environment and Fisheries.
While this year in the Atlantic area there is an expenditure of $12 million on maintenance and public works, according to these people there should be an expenditure of $30 million. In the committee, these officials told us that in order to satisfy the needs of the Atlantic area and to bring it up to a level where fishermen would be able to fish successfully, with adequate facilities, there should be an expenditure of at least $100 million. We appreciate the need for more, and bigger and better buildings in Ottawa and in Ontario generally and in other parts of Canada, and we appreciate the need for bigger and better air-conditioning units, bigger and better cafeterias and bigger and better parking structures. We are not against these because we recognize that, this being the seat of government, certain amenities must be provided for our public servants.
June 4, 1973

But speaking for my riding, I think I am echoing the sentiments of most people in the Atlantic area when I say that we cannot accept the fact that this government and our present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube), in conjunction with the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries, have obviously placed a greater priority on building office towers in Ottawa and the amenities to which I have just referred than providing facilities to enable our fishermen in the Atlantic area, especially in Newfoundland and my riding, to be able successfully to prosecute the fishery.
It is a little alarming to find we have a government which is more interested in spending, or at least in committing itself to an expenditure of $36 million on a new building for the Department of Finance, and Treasury Board in Ottawa than it is in providing these badly needed facilities in the Atlantic region or indeed in maintaining the present facilities. We have the Minister of Public Works presiding over a department which has permitted properties in eastern Canada, especially in Newfoundland, to deteriorate to a point where in many cases they have been marked as being unsafe for people to travel on or reside in.
Can you imagine parts of Newfoundland-and I have seen this-where fishing is so vital to the economy of the province, where it is the mainstay of the people who live in that area, where barriers are erected on public wharves advising people not to bring their vehicles there because it is unsafe? This is a government that pleads poverty when it comes to providing these facilities, but is able to spend this year in excess of $25 million on providing other facilities for the bureaucracy in Ottawa and upper Canada. This is hard to take. Of course, some of the blame, perhaps all of the blame should be placed on the shoulders of the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries because he is obviously now more concerned with imposing regulations and restrictions on fishermen than with helping them to increase their catches and their earnings.
