speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Carter) may not be aware of the fact that the federal taxpayer spends more money by far on the fishing industry, per dollar of profit per employee, than any other industry in Canada. This is the case today. It has been the case for a number of years. Therefore, as Minister of Fisheries I make no apology to him or anyone else for the level of federal assistance to fishermen.
In recent years a number of departments have been involved in assisting fisheries, the most notable of which is the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. In the last half dozen years there has been a fantastic growth of fish processing facilities. The hon. member knows that, the fishermen know that well, and the industry certainly is aware of it. Also, in the last three years there has been a remarkable increase in the number of new fishing boats built. At the moment there are far more fishing vessels in
Adjournment Debate
total being built in this country than at any time in the history of the industry. In that case, as well, there is a 35 per cent subsidy for practically all of those vessels.
So, one, in respect of processing and, two, in respect of vessels and gear there has been a remarkable expansion in the public effort in support of fishermen. We are now going into the third phase because bigger vessels are being built and we need different kinds of docks and wharves. I will be the first to admit that we have not put anything like the effort into looking after small craft harbours as we must do in the next few years to look after these new vessels and to make sure that fish flow efficiently from the boats to the plants.
The total budget of the Fisheries Service in Canada is now approaching $100 million. A very large proportion of that budget is spent in the province of Newfoundland. I wish the hon. member had referred to figures of that kind rather than to public buildings which are of little direct use to the fishermen of Newfoundland in any case.

subtopic: ENERGY-POSSIBLE ESTABLISHMENT OF REFINERY AT GROS CACOUNA-FEDERAL GOVERNMENT PARTICIPATION WITH QUEBEC IN DISCUSSIONS WITH SAUDI ARABIA
ENERGY-POSSIBLE ESTABLISHMENT OF REFINERY AT GROS CACOUNA-FEDERAL GOVERNMENT PARTICIPATION WITH QUEBEC IN DISCUSSIONS WITH SAUDI ARABIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some time last week I began asking a series of questions of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) with regard to the proposed construction of a supertanker port in the Gros Cacouna-Ile Verte region in the St. Lawrence River region of Quebec. Needless to say, I was not thoroughly satisfied with the answers and that is why I am up again tonight to pursue the matter.
Particularly with regard to the question I asked on May 29, the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, we have already completed an environmental impact assessment on the Lorneville project in New Brunswick, and a joint investigation regarding the Canso project is under way. We are happy to join with the provinces in these kinds of appraisals at any time.
The point, of course, is that although this was a satisfying answer to some, it was not an answer to the question I was asking, which was with regard to the proposed construction of a supertanker port at Gros Cacouna-Ile Verte. Obviously, this is not a very good area in which to build a supertanker port. At that point the St. Lawrence becomes quite narrow; the tidal currents are very strong and extremely variable. On both sides the river has shallow waters, and in the middle of the river there is a dangerous little island called Red Islet. Knowing that supertankers can take ten miles to come to a dead stop, one wonders whether putting a supertanker port in that area is an idea, or somebody's bad dream.
I have an indication that the minister may be worried about this project, from reading a letter of his which was printed in the Globe and Mail last Saturday in which he wrote, among many other things:
So why run the danger of messing up our beautiful Gulf islands?
These are the west coast Gulf islands he was talking about.
Why run the risk of polluting a scenic area which is many times

June 4, 1973
Adjournment Debate
more valuable than the Thousand Islands on the St. Lawrence River?
How he compares the Gulf islands with the St. Lawrence Islands, I do not know. Further in his letter he wrote:
The idea of bringing 250,000 ton tankers into a narrow channel such as that approaching Eastport, Maine, is ridiculous, not only from an environmental but also from a navigational point of view. The same applies to ports well up the St. Lawrence River. We mustn't be stupid about these things.
He does not specify what "well up" is. I do not think he uses the term "well up" in the sense that Alice used it in "Alice in Wonderland." I would like to know if the minister is fearful of the project at Gros Cacouna-Ile Verte, and why he has been wary about answering questions put to him directly. Indeed, in the past some of the officials in his department have been more forthright. In an article printed in the Ottawa Citizen of December 6, 1972, Robert F. Shaw, deputy environment minister, said:
Ports for supertankers shouldn't be built without major studies into possible environmental effects.
In the article he went on to point out that there were considerable fears about building a port at Gros Cacouna-Ile Verte. We know there has been a certain amount of artful dodging, I am not saying here on the part of the minister, but between the federal government and the provincial government over this matter. The Minister of Industry and Commerce in Quebec has said, unsaid, and resaid on several occasions, in October, November and December, 1972, and again this year, that federal approval had been given for the building of this port. I have tried to find out on two occasions, once from the acting prime minister and once from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), whether federal approval had been given, and which department of government had given that approval. So far I have received no answer. I do not expect an answer on this particular point tonight from the Minister of the Environment, but I would not mind having an answer soon.
Just to end off my question, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister specifically whether he intends to proceed with serious ecological studies of the lower St. Lawrence, particularly in view of two facts. The first is the immense danger posed to those extremely valuable and historic waters of ours if there were a major oil spill, and the second is with a view to using the St. Lawrence as a source of aquaculture. I did not say "agriculture," but "aquaculture". We all know that we are suffering a food shortage in the world and that the food shortage will become worse. One wonders whether it is wise to doom a source of food supply such as the St. Lawrence to complete sterility forever, rather than proceed to develop its natural capacity to produce food for us and for the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENERGY-POSSIBLE ESTABLISHMENT OF REFINERY AT GROS CACOUNA-FEDERAL GOVERNMENT PARTICIPATION WITH QUEBEC IN DISCUSSIONS WITH SAUDI ARABIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Harney) knows, no port is absolutely safe and no development is absolutely safe from an environmental point of view; they vary a great deal, one compared with another. We have not carried out exhaustive environmental studies in the general area of Gros Cacouna-Ile Verte. The principal developer has begun to carry out the necessary investi-[Mr. Harney.l
gations. The company has been in touch with our officials with a view to determining what criteria, what guidelines, what tests we would apply in assessing ports of that general character.
I understand that the developers will be completing some of these studies using basic data supplied by the Department of the Environment for Canada, and relevant Quebec government departments as well, within the next two or three months. This fits in very well with the approach we are taking generally-the developer must present his case showing the advantages of the development, must look at the environmental aspects of the development as well as its economic aspects, navigation, the risks inherent in sailing through those waters and the risks to surrounding industries including fisheries, tourism, and so on. We do not have an adequate report on tanker offloading and onloading development in the stretch of the St. Lawrence River in the vicinity of lie Verte-Gros Cacouna. We are working with the developer and we will see what the results are.

HARBOURS-LADNER, B.C.-REQUEST FOR DREDGING TO ASSIST FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I first started asking questions about the Ladner harbour the hon. minister did not seem to know what the problem was, so I asked to be put on the ten o'clock debate. Better than telling the House in my own words what some of the problems are in the harbour, I should like to read into the record a letter from Mr. Edgar A. Birch, a fisherman in the area and a member of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union, local No. 4. It was a letter to the editor and it reads as follows:
Editor,
Once again we have seen stupidity carried out to its fullest by the Fraser River Harbour Commission-that body of people who are answerable to no one, except Ottawa, since they are appointed and not elected.
Three years ago, myself and Nick Spilchen, who are fishermen, and two aldermen, met with this commission at the Delta Municipal Hall.
We pointed out to the commissioner that it was useless to go on this way without a plan, as to what we are going to do with the harbour and where to put the sand when dredging is done.
They agreed that even a couple of fishermen could be right.
They went away and that was the last we saw of them. However, a year ago, an engineer from the Department of Public Works showed up in Ladner. We showed this man what we wanted done in Ladner, and we pointed out that the slough would have to be widened to 300 feet, twice its present width. He agreed and said it was no problem from an engineer's point of view.
Eight months ago we started asking for the slough to be dredged again as it was filled up at the mouth to the point where you couldn't get in at low tide with any boat that draws over four feet of water.
Just about each month they informed us they were too busy, until March when we took the Member of Parliament, John Reynolds, on a trip of the river. Two weeks later we were informed that Ladner slough would be dredged. It seems that Reynolds did his homework in Ottawa. However, all consultation ended there.
The dredge came into Ladner and no one consulted the fishermen or the council as to what should be done, and went ahead and dredged the sand up along the edge of the slough and left it there.
June 4, 1973

Now if we want the slough widened, as we proposed, we will have to move two weeks' of dredging to do so.
If they had put it another 300 yards further inland it would have come to good use later on.
This we are supposed to call an intelligent harbour commission which consults no one. It is time this body was elected and answerable to the public if we are ever going to get anywhere on the Fraser River.
The icing on the cake came when an official assured the fishermen that the channel was dredged enough and they were leaving. The dredge only went about 400 yards when it went aground and stayed there three and a half hours until the tide came in enough to float it.
This once again shows the stupidity of this commission.
Edgar A. Birch
Mr. Speaker, I went up to the slough again last week and took five Members of Parliament with me to show them what the area should be like. It should have better docks. Fishermen are told by the companies, "You can use our facilities for free". But they must give away sometimes 5 per cent or 10 per cent of their bonuses every year to pay for these dock facilities. That can amount to quite a bit more than their competitors to the south, across the border, pay. They can go to the finest port facilities and for $200 or $300 per year keep their boats there.
This government is spending in excess of $100 million in British Columbia on ports this year, and yet is not touching Ladner or sloughs or small fishing ports in the area. We want to know why. The fishermen in the area want to know why, because they are the mainstay of the economy of the area. We demand that some action be taken with respect to sloughs and docks in that area.
